_note: How to use each simulation. The control names are taken from the simulation's actual English UI strings. Changing the language changes the names inside the simulation too, so a translation has to match the names in that language's UI strings.

_common.intro: All 61 PhET sims are built to the same rules. Learn these eight things and you won't get lost in a sim you have never opened before.

sections.name: The black bar along the bottom
sections.desc: Every sim has one. On the left are the house button and the screen names; at the far right is the PhET logo.
sections.tip: The house button and the screen names show up only in sims with more than one screen. If you cannot see them, that sim has just one screen.

sections.name: The house button — choosing a screen
sections.desc: One sim often holds several screens. Press the house button to go back to the list of screens and pick a different one.
sections.tip: Each screen covers something different. When a lesson names a screen we open that one for you, so if nothing is specified, start on the first screen.

sections.name: The round reset button, bottom right
sections.desc: It puts every setting back the way it started. It is the yellow circle at the bottom right of the sim.
sections.tip: Press this first when you are stuck. It is the quickest fix when you have lost track of what you changed. It only clears settings inside the sim — what you wrote in ④ stays where it is.

sections.name: The group of checkboxes at the top right
sections.desc: These are switches for things you cannot see. Electric fields, velocity arrows, gridlines, numeric values — whatever is normally hidden is gathered here.
sections.tip: Nine times out of ten, "I cannot see anything" is solved right here. When you open a sim, turn every checkbox on once. You will find out what that sim is able to show you.

sections.name: Play, pause, and speed
sections.desc: Only in sims where time runs. The triangle is play and the two bars are pause, with buttons beside them for Slow · Normal · Fast.
sections.tip: If it moves too fast to follow, set it to Slow and watch again. You can still change values while it is paused, so stopping the sim, setting up your conditions and then pressing play makes things far easier to watch.

sections.name: Sliders (the bar you drag)
sections.desc: Grab the handle and drag. When you need an exact value, click the handle once and then use the left and right arrow keys.
sections.tip: Shift + arrow moves in smaller steps and Page Up/Down in larger ones. A value you cannot hit with the mouse is easy to hit from the keyboard.

sections.name: The PhET logo menu (far right)
sections.desc: Press the logo and you get items such as Options… (sound, color contrast and so on), Screenshot, Full Screen and About…. Which items appear differs a little from sim to sim.
sections.tip: Rather than the Full Screen in here, use the Fullscreen button above this page. It brings you back to exactly the place in the lesson you left.

sections.name: Working with the keyboard alone
sections.desc: Tab for the next item, Shift+Tab for the previous one, Space or Enter to press, arrow keys to change a value. For an object you drag, press Space to grab it, move it with the arrows, then press Space again to drop it.
sections.tip: Some sims have a button in the bottom bar that opens a list of Keyboard Shortcuts. Any special key that exists only in that sim — jumping to the wall, for instance — is written there.

balloons-and-static-electricity.summary: Rub a balloon on a sweater to build up static, then watch it stick to the wall - down to the individual charges. There is only one screen, so the bottom bar has no house button. The sweater is on the left, the wall on the right, the balloon in the middle.

controls.name: The balloon (drag it around)
controls.desc: Grab the balloon and rub it over the sweater, and negative charge moves from the sweater onto the balloon.
controls.tip: Do not rub once and hard - go back and forth slowly, several times. You can watch the charges cross one at a time. Let go and the balloon is pulled back on its own.

controls.name: Show all charges · Show no charges · Show charge differences (bottom left)
controls.desc: These are radio buttons - only one at a time. Unlike checkboxes, you cannot have several on at once.
controls.tip: Start on Show all charges to see what is happening, then switch to Show charge differences to see just the outcome. Matched pairs vanish and only the leftovers stay.

controls.name: Remove Wall (bottom right)
controls.desc: Takes the wall on the right away. Once it is gone, the button in the same place turns into the one that brings the wall back.
controls.tip: Take the wall away, rub up some charge, then put the wall back. You get to see the exact moment it sticks.

controls.name: One balloon · two balloons (bottom center, two panels of balloon pictures)
controls.desc: Two panels with balloons drawn on them. Press the right-hand one and a second, green balloon appears. The panels carry pictures only, no words.
controls.tip: Rub both so they carry the same sign, then bring them close. They push each other away.

controls.name: Reset Balloon
controls.desc: Puts only the balloon back - its position and its charge.
controls.tip: The round yellow reset at the bottom right puts back the wall and the display setting as well. When you only want the balloons again, use this one.

steps: Check that Show all charges is selected.
Drag the balloon over the sweater and work it slowly back and forth. Watch what crosses - only the −, never the +.
Bring the rubbed balloon close to the wall. Watch how the charges at the surface of the wall arrange themselves.
Switch to Show charge differences and see which one ended up positive, the sweater or the balloon.
Pick the two-balloon panel, rub them both, and bring them near each other.
gotchas: Even with the balloon stuck to it, the wall carries no charge. The charges inside the wall have only moved seats.
The thing that moves is always negative charge. Positive charge stays put. Miss this and everything after it gets confusing.
Hold the balloon against something without rubbing and nothing happens. That is not a fault.

charges-and-fields.summary: Drop charges into empty space and watch, in arrows, how the space around them changes. There is only one screen, so the bottom bar has no house button.

controls.name: The tray at the bottom - +1 nC · -1 nC · Sensors
controls.desc: Drag them out of the tray to place them. Red +1 nC is a positive charge, blue -1 nC a negative one, and the yellow dot is a sensor.
controls.tip: To clear one away, drag it back onto the tray. The moment a charge lands, the arrows around it come alive.

controls.name: Electric Field (top right · on by default)
controls.desc: Lays a dense carpet of little arrows over the whole screen. With no charges out they are faint; place a charge and they turn bright and large around it.
controls.tip: The size and brightness of an arrow is the strength. Without measuring anything you can see that it weakens fast with distance.

controls.name: Direction Only
controls.desc: Indented one step under Electric Field. Makes every arrow the same length and leaves only the direction.
controls.tip: Turn it on when the strengths are so different that the arrows are too long or too short to read a direction from.

controls.name: Voltage · Values · Grid
controls.desc: Voltage paints the screen in colors by voltage, Values shows the numbers alongside, and Grid lays a grid on the floor.
controls.tip: Snap to Grid below only wakes up once Grid is on - that is why it sits greyed out. With it on, charges click onto the grid and distances are easy to set.

controls.name: The voltage sensor (middle right · upper slot)
controls.desc: Drag it out and it reads the voltage at that spot as a number, like 0.0 V. Press the button on the sensor and it draws the line joining every point at that same voltage.
controls.tip: Move along one of those lines and the value never changes, however far you go. Seeing that for yourself is what makes the word "equipotential" click.

controls.name: The measuring tape (middle right · lower slot)
controls.desc: Pull the yellow reel out and it measures the distance between two points.
controls.tip: Use it for any mission that says "exactly twice the distance". By eye you cannot tell a quarter from a half.

steps: Drag one red +1 nC into the middle of the screen.
Check that the arrows around it get smaller and fainter with distance.
Measure a distance with the measuring tape and put a sensor there. Remember the arrow length.
Move that same sensor twice as far out. See whether it is half, or less than half.
Add a blue -1 nC facing it and put a sensor between the two charges.
Take readings at a few spots with the voltage sensor and draw the equipotential lines.
gotchas: An arrow means the force a positive charge would feel if you put one there. It does not mean something is there now feeling a force.
Get very close to a charge and the arrows grow long enough to run off the screen. Not a fault - it really is that strong.
If Snap to Grid will not take a press, Grid is switched off.
Charges dropped on top of each other make the arithmetic look strange. Set them a little apart.

coulombs-law.summary: Measure the force between two charges as a number. This sim starts at the screen chooser - open it and you get two screen panels first, not the experiment.

screens.name: Macro Scale
screens.what: Two objects at a size you can see, in cm and μC. Start here.

screens.name: Atomic Scale
screens.what: Whether the same rule still holds at atomic size (pm, e). The controls are identical; only the units change.

controls.name: The two charged objects, q₁ and q₂ (drag them)
controls.desc: Drag an object left or right and the distance changes; the force arrow and the number follow immediately.
controls.tip: This is the main thing you do here. Change the distance and leave the charges alone - that is how the rule shows itself.

controls.name: The ruler (already lying on the screen)
controls.desc: Drag it against the two objects to measure the distance exactly. It is out from the start; you do not have to fetch it.
controls.tip: To make the distance exactly double, you have to use the ruler. By eye the rule stays invisible.

controls.name: Charge 1 · Charge 2 (value box and slider)
controls.desc: Run from −10 to 10. They go negative as well.
controls.tip: The ◀ ▶ beside the value box step one notch at a time. Dragging the slider makes round numbers hard to hit.

controls.name: Force Values - Decimal Notation · Scientific Notation · Hidden (right)
controls.desc: Radio buttons, one at a time. Choose Hidden and the numbers go away, leaving only the arrows.
controls.tip: When the value is so small it reads 0.0000…, Scientific Notation is easier. When you want to guess by feel before leaning on the numbers, leave it on Hidden.

controls.name: The figures hauling on the two objects
controls.desc: They act out the size of the force. Not a control, but the most important picture in this sim.
controls.tip: However different the charges are, both figures pull with the same force. The fact that the bigger side does not feel a stronger pull is drawn right there.

steps: At the screen chooser, press Macro Scale.
Set the distance to 2 cm with the ruler and write down the force value.
Leave the charges alone and stretch the distance to 4 cm. Work out what fraction of the force is left.
Go back to 2 cm, then double only the size of Charge 1 (−4 → −8 μC). How many times bigger is it this time?
Make one of the charges negative and see what happens to the direction of the arrows.
Use the house button to visit Atomic Scale and check that the same rule holds.
gotchas: Touch the charges while you are changing the distance and the rule stays hidden. Change one thing at a time.
The force arrows sit on both objects, the same size in opposite directions. The bigger charge does not feel a stronger force.
Bring the distance close to 0 and the value explodes. That is the limit of the sim, not an error.
Do not be thrown when no experiment appears as you open it. This one asks you to pick a screen first.

faradays-electromagnetic-lab.summary: Make electricity with a magnet and a coil. There are five screens, so it opens on the screen chooser and you move between them with the house button in the bottom bar. The tools differ from screen to screen - read the screen list below first.

screens.name: Bar Magnet
screens.what: Just a magnet, to look at the shape of the field. See Inside and Flip Polarity exist only on this screen.

screens.name: Pickup Coil
screens.what: Move a magnet near a coil to make electricity. This is the key screen for this course, and Indicator, Loops and Lock to Axis all live here.

screens.name: Electromagnet
screens.what: The other way round: run electricity through and make a magnet.

screens.name: Transformer
screens.what: Two coils facing each other, moving electricity across.

screens.name: Generator
screens.what: A water wheel spins the magnet to make electricity continuously. This is how a power station works.

controls.name: Magnetic Field (B) - every screen · on by default
controls.desc: Fills the background with a dense field of little compass needles showing the shape of the magnetic field.
controls.tip: Turn it off and the space around the magnet looks empty. It shows you that a field is not something you see but something the sim draws for you.

controls.name: Strength (bar magnet panel · 75% by default)
controls.desc: Sets how strong the magnet is, from 0 to 100%.
controls.tip: Take it down to 0 and back up and you can see exactly how the field display responds.

controls.name: See Inside · Flip Polarity - Bar Magnet screen only
controls.desc: See Inside shows the inside of the magnet; Flip Polarity swaps N and S.
controls.tip: It is easy to hunt for these two on the Pickup Coil screen. They are not there. To reverse the direction, run the magnet through the other way instead.

controls.name: Indicator - bulb · meter (Pickup Coil screen)
controls.desc: Chooses what hangs off the coil. The bulb shows only brightness; the meter shows direction too. Both options are pictures, with no words on them.
controls.tip: To see that "in and out are opposite" you have to switch to the meter. The bulb lights the same either way the current runs.

controls.name: Loops · Loop Area (Pickup Coil screen)
controls.desc: How many turns the coil has, and how wide you make it.
controls.tip: Two ways to get more electricity without a stronger magnet. This is why a real generator winds its coil thousands of times.

controls.name: Lock to Axis (Pickup Coil screen)
controls.desc: Pins the magnet so it can only move left and right.
controls.tip: If your hand slips and the magnet wanders up and down, the results get messy. Turn it on before you start.

controls.name: Compass · Field Meter
controls.desc: Tick these and the tool appears on screen. The Compass gives you the field direction at that spot; the Field Meter gives you the strength as a number.
controls.tip: Walk the compass slowly once around the magnet. You can see where the field comes out and where it goes back in.

steps: On the Bar Magnet screen, walk the compass once around the magnet to see the shape of the field.
Use the house button to go to Pickup Coil and turn on Lock to Axis.
Push the magnet slowly into the coil. What does the bulb do?
Hold the magnet completely still inside the coil - this one observation is the whole sim.
Now run it through quickly. What is different from the slow pass?
Switch Indicator to the meter and check the direction going in against coming out.
Raise Loops and Loop Area and run it again at the same speed.
Finish on the Generator screen, watching water keep the magnet turning.
gotchas: A magnet held still makes no electricity. It is not about the magnet being strong; it has to move. Miss this and everything else comes out wrong.
The tools differ from screen to screen. See Inside and Flip Polarity are on Bar Magnet; Indicator, Loops and Lock to Axis are on Pickup Coil.
The bulb tells you nothing about the direction of the electricity. Switch to the meter for that.
If the bulb only glows very faintly, turn up the strength or move the magnet faster. It is not broken.

projectile-motion.summary: Fire things out of a cannon and watch where they land and how long they take. Change the angle, the speed, the object and the air resistance until the rule shows itself.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. The simplest screen - only the angle and the speed to change.

screens.name: Vectors
screens.what: Shows velocity and acceleration as arrows. Splitting them into horizontal and vertical is the heart of this lesson.

screens.name: Drag
screens.what: The air resistance screen. "Drag" here does not mean hauling something along - it is the resistance of the air.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: Type in the numbers yourself: height, angle, speed, mass, diameter, even gravity.

controls.name: Cannon Angle · Initial Speed (bottom of the screen)
controls.desc: Set the launch angle and the starting speed. You can press the number field and type a value in.
controls.tip: Change one at a time. Change the angle and the speed together and you will never know which one moved the result.

controls.name: Cannon height (drag the cannon up and down)
controls.desc: Drag the cannon upward and the launch height changes. The scale on the left shows the height.
controls.tip: To compare dropping against throwing you have to keep the same height. Set it against the scale.

controls.name: Time · Range · Height (readouts at the top)
controls.desc: Time is how long the flight took, Range how far it went, Height the top of the arc.
controls.tip: The value that matters most in this lesson is Time. Changing the speed without changing the time is the whole point, so write it down every run.

controls.name: Velocity Vectors - Total · Components (right of the Vectors screen)
controls.desc: Choose whether to see the velocity as one arrow or split into horizontal and vertical.
controls.tip: Do turn on Components. That the horizontal arrow keeps its length while only the vertical one grows is this entire lesson.

controls.name: Acceleration Vectors (right of the Vectors screen)
controls.desc: Shows the acceleration as an arrow.
controls.tip: It points straight down for the whole flight, including while the ball is still going up. That is an easy one to get wrong.

controls.name: Air Resistance (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Tick it and the air is taken into the calculation. The Drag Coefficient underneath is how much the object catches the air.
controls.tip: Leave it off to begin with. Get hold of the bare rule first, then switch it on and see what moves.

controls.name: Projectile chooser (right)
controls.desc: Cannonball, golf ball, baseball, football, pumpkin, human, piano, car and more. The mass and the diameter change with your choice.
controls.tip: With air resistance off, every one of them flies the same path. It takes air to make a difference - which is a good check in itself.

controls.name: Measuring tape (bottom left)
controls.desc: Drag it out to measure between two points.
controls.tip: The screen scale only gets you an estimate. When you need the real value, use the tape.

controls.name: Eraser · pause · step buttons and the speed setting (bottom)
controls.desc: Clear the trails, stop the action, advance one frame, and change the playback speed. All of these are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: Set the speed to Slow and walk forward one frame at a time with the step button, and you can see exactly how the arrows change.

steps: Turn Air Resistance off.
Set the cannon to Height 10 m, Cannon Angle 0°.
Fire at Initial Speed 0 and note the Time.
Fire at Initial Speed 15, then 25, and compare the times.
On the Vectors screen turn on Velocity Vectors → Components and watch the arrows.
Work the angle from 15° to 75°, noting the Range, and find the best angle.
Turn Air Resistance on and see whether the best angle moves.
gotchas: The screen called Drag is about air resistance, not about dragging things. The Drag Coefficient below is the air resistance coefficient.
With air resistance off, everything flies the same path whatever you fire. That is not a fault; it is the correct answer.
The acceleration arrow points down even while the ball is rising.
There are four screens. Start on Intro and move to Vectors.

projectile-data-lab.summary: It looks like the previous sim but the purpose is different. Not where one shot lands but how many shots scatter. That is why there is a histogram across the top.

screens.name: Variability
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Fire repeatedly on one setting and look at the scatter.

screens.name: Sources
screens.what: Where the scatter comes from - the launcher or the projectile - pulled apart.

screens.name: Measures
screens.what: You can switch on Mean and Standard Deviation here. The back half of this lesson happens on this screen.

screens.name: Sampling
screens.what: Fire in batches and then look at the means of those batches. The hardest screen.

controls.name: Single · Continuous (bottom center)
controls.desc: Single fires one at a time; Continuous keeps firing while you hold it.
controls.tip: Fire five or six on Single first to see that every one is different, then collect dozens with Continuous.

controls.name: Launch Angle · Launch Speed (checkboxes, top right)
controls.desc: Tick these and the launch angle and speed are displayed on screen. Unlike the previous sim these are not handles that set the values - the launcher on the Variability screen is a Mystery Launcher with its settings hidden.
controls.tip: In this lesson, do not change them. Firing on a fixed setting is the whole point.

controls.name: Histogram (top of the screen)
controls.desc: Counts the landing distances into intervals and stacks them as bars. The horizontal axis is Distance, the vertical axis is Count.
controls.tip: Stack up dozens of shots and a bell, high in the middle, comes out. Ten or so will not show it, so fire plenty.

controls.name: Bin Width · Total Bins (left of the histogram)
controls.desc: Sets how wide an interval each bar counts.
controls.tip: Same data, different-looking shape. Chop it too finely and it goes ragged; too coarsely and the shape is smeared away.

controls.name: Paths (right)
controls.desc: Leaves the flight trails on the screen.
controls.tip: Leave it on and you can see at a glance how much the paths overlap and how far they spread.

controls.name: Mean · Standard Deviation (right of the Measures screen)
controls.desc: Mean shows where they cluster, Standard Deviation how wide the spread is.
controls.tip: Add shots and watch the mean line settle. With few shots it wanders; with many it takes its place.

controls.name: Mystery Launcher · Custom Launcher
controls.desc: Mystery will not tell you how much scatter it has. Custom lets you set it yourself.
controls.tip: Fire the mystery one, guess its scatter, then build the same value on the custom launcher and compare. Good practice.

controls.name: Measuring Tape · Stopwatch · Interval Tool (right)
controls.desc: Measure distance and time, and count how many shots fell inside a given stretch.
controls.tip: Set the Interval Tool to a narrow stretch around the mean. More shots fall inside it than you would think.

steps: On the Variability screen, change nothing and fire five or six on Single.
Collect dozens with Continuous and look at the shape of the histogram.
Change the Bin Width and see the same data look different.
Turn on Paths and see how far the trails spread.
On the Measures screen turn on Mean and Standard Deviation.
Add shots and watch the mean line settle.
gotchas: The point of this sim is not changing the settings. Touch the angle or the speed and there is no scatter to see.
Ten or so shots will not show the shape. Collect dozens.
Changing the Bin Width leaves the data alone. Only the grouping changes.
The screens get harder as you go. Variability → Measures is enough for this lesson.

energy-skate-park.summary: Put a skater on a track and watch, in bars, how the energy moves around. You can draw your own track, and you can swap gravity for the Moon or Jupiter.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Ready-made tracks, and the energy bars.

screens.name: Measure
screens.what: Adds a tape, a stopwatch and an energy probe. You can move the Reference Height here too.

screens.name: Graphs
screens.what: The energies drawn as a graph against time.

screens.name: Playground
screens.what: Draw your own track. A good place to play once you are done.

controls.name: The skater (drag onto the track)
controls.desc: Drop the skater at any height on the track and they slide from there.
controls.tip: Try dropping from the same height several times. Different track shapes, same height, same speed.

controls.name: Energy bars (collapsible box, top left) - Kinetic · Potential · Thermal · Total
controls.desc: It opens collapsed, showing only the title. Press ▸ to open it. Kinetic is the energy of speed, Potential the energy of height, Thermal the share lost to friction, and Total the sum of the three.
controls.tip: This is the key readout. Do not take your eyes off the Total bar. With no friction it must be the same height wherever the skater is.

controls.name: Friction (right) - None ↔ Lots
controls.desc: Sets the friction of the track.
controls.tip: Start on None. With friction on, conservation of energy comes out blurred. Get hold of the rule first, then switch it on.

controls.name: Track chooser (right, four picture buttons)
controls.desc: Four ready-made tracks. There are no words on them - you tell them apart by the shape of the track drawn on each: in order, a parabola, a ramp, a double dip and a loop.
controls.tip: The double dip is the best one for watching the energy trade. The skater runs from side to side, swapping height for speed.

controls.name: Stick to Track (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: On, the skater stays glued to the track; off, they can fly off it.
controls.tip: Turn it off on the loop track. Without enough speed the skater falls - which is why a real loop-the-loop needs to be taken fast.

controls.name: Gravity (right) - Earth · Moon · Jupiter · Custom
controls.desc: Changes the strength of gravity.
controls.tip: Try the Moon. Same track, far slower motion. What matters is that the Total still holds.

controls.name: Mass (right)
controls.desc: Changes how heavy the skater is.
controls.tip: With no friction, changing the mass does not change how high they get. Only the size of the bars changes - a good thing to check.

controls.name: Pie Chart (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Shows the energy split as a circle. It follows the skater around.
controls.tip: The bars give you the exact amounts, the pie gives you the proportions. Having both on makes it click faster.

controls.name: Reference Height (Measure screen) · Grid
controls.desc: Sets where you call zero for potential energy.
controls.tip: Move it and every potential energy value shifts. It is there to show you that the difference matters, not the value.

controls.name: Restart Skater · the clear-thermal button
controls.desc: Put the skater back where they started, or clear the heat that has piled up. The clear-thermal button sits on the energy box as an icon, with no words on it.
controls.tip: When you run several friction experiments, clear the heat before each one. Otherwise the last run's heat is still there.

steps: Set Friction to None and press ▸ on the Energy box at the top left to open it.
Put the skater on the high side of the track and watch the bars move back and forth.
Check that the Total bar is the same everywhere.
Compare the highest point on the far side with the height you started from.
Raise Friction and watch the Thermal bar grow.
Change Gravity to Moon and do it all again.
On the Measure screen, move the Reference Height.
gotchas: The track buttons have no words on them. You tell them apart by the shape drawn on each: parabola, ramp, double dip, loop.
With friction on the Total looks as if it is shrinking, but count the Thermal bar too and it is unchanged.
Clear the heat before you repeat a friction experiment.
Changing the mass does not change how high they get, as long as there is no friction.
Moving the Reference Height changes the potential energy values. Not an error - the baseline moved.

vector-addition.summary: Drag arrows onto a graph and add them up. See with your own eyes how quantities that carry a direction combine. Only Sum · Values · Components are labelled in words; the rest of the buttons carry pictures and no text at all.

screens.name: Explore 1D
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Vectors sit on a single line. Two directions only, so it is the simplest.

screens.name: Explore 2D
screens.what: Vectors can point any way at all. The heart of this lesson is here.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: Put several vectors out and handle them freely.

screens.name: Equations
screens.what: Relationships between vectors, written as equations. The hardest screen.

controls.name: Vector drawer (right) - a · b · c
controls.desc: Drag a lettered arrow onto the graph. Once it is down, drag its tip to change the size and the direction.
controls.tip: Drag the body of an arrow to move it, drag the tip to resize and turn it. When in doubt, grab the tip.

controls.name: Sum (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Shows the sum vector of everything you have put down.
controls.tip: The star of this sim. Leave it on and turn a vector. How the size of the sum changes is this whole lesson.

controls.name: Values (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Puts the size of each vector on screen as a number.
controls.tip: By eye you cannot land exactly on 3 and 4. Turn it on.

controls.name: Show angles (top right, the θ picture checkbox)
controls.desc: Marks the angle each vector makes with the x axis.
controls.tip: When you are hunting for where the sum is largest and smallest, seeing the angle makes the rule obvious.

controls.name: Components (top right, four picture buttons)
controls.desc: Splits a vector into horizontal and vertical. Four pictures in a 2×2 block with no words, running from the top left: off, right triangle, parallelogram, and dotted lines dropped onto the axes.
controls.tip: Choose the bottom right picture, the one with dotted lines down to the axes. It is the same picture as splitting the velocity into horizontal and vertical in lesson 1 (projectile motion).

controls.name: Grid (top right, the graph-paper picture checkbox)
controls.desc: Turns the background grid on and off.
controls.tip: Leave it on. Without the grid you cannot set the sizes exactly.

controls.name: Coordinate chooser (bottom right, two picture buttons)
controls.desc: On the 1D screen it picks horizontal or vertical; on the 2D screen it picks grid coordinates or angle coordinates. There are no words - the right-triangle picture is grid coordinates, the fan-of-angles picture is angle coordinates.
controls.tip: Switch to the fan-of-angles one and you get an angle scale, which makes 30° or 45° easy to hit exactly.

controls.name: Erase all vectors (bottom right, picture button)
controls.desc: Clears every vector you have put down.
controls.tip: When the arrows overlap and you lose track, clearing and starting again is quicker.

controls.name: Vector Values (readout at the top)
controls.desc: Shows the size and angle of the vector you have selected. With nothing selected it reads No vector selected.
controls.tip: To see the values you have to click an arrow once to select it.

steps: On the Explore 1D screen turn on Values and the grid (the graph-paper picture checkbox).
Put vector a down at size 3 and b at size 4, both pointing right.
Turn on Sum and look at the size of the sum.
Flip b the other way and see what the sum does.
On the Explore 2D screen, turn one of them slowly.
Set the two at right angles and check the sum comes to 5.
Switch the Components picture buttons to the bottom right one, the dotted lines down to the axes.
gotchas: Most of the buttons have no words on them. They are pictures, not English text you have missed - use the names above to work out which picture is which.
Vector sizes cannot simply be added. 3 and 4 make 7 only when they point the same way.
Dragging an arrow's body moves it; dragging its tip changes the size and direction.
To see the values you have to click an arrow to select it.
This sim was built for high school. This lesson only uses Explore 1D and Explore 2D.

hookes-law.summary: Pull or press a spring and watch the relationship between force and stretch. Nothing here moves, so the controls are very simple - one handle is nearly all of it.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. One spring, force against stretch.

screens.name: Systems
screens.what: Put two springs side by side or end to end.

screens.name: Energy
screens.what: Shows the stored energy as bars and as a plot. The heart of this lesson is here.

controls.name: Applied Force (handle at the bottom)
controls.desc: Sets the force you put on the spring. Push it right to pull, left to compress.
controls.tip: The main thing you do here. Land on round values (0.1 m, 0.2 m) and write them down, or the rule stays hidden.

controls.name: Spring Constant (handle at the bottom)
controls.desc: Sets how stiff the spring is. Bigger means it stretches less.
controls.tip: Apply the same force and double the constant. The stretch goes to half - the two are inversely proportional.

controls.name: Applied Force · Spring Force (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Draws the two forces as arrows.
controls.tip: Turn both on. They are the same size in opposite directions. That picture is what "a spring gives back what you put in" means.

controls.name: Displacement · Equilibrium Position · Values (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Displacement is how far it stretched, Equilibrium Position is where it sits at zero force, and Values puts the numbers on screen.
controls.tip: Do turn Values on. By eye you cannot tell twice from four times.

controls.name: Bar Graph and Energy Plot (right of the Energy screen)
controls.desc: Shows the stored elastic energy as a bar and as a curve.
controls.tip: Look hard at the shape of the plot. Force is a straight line but energy is curved - the parabola from lesson 12.

controls.name: Spring arrangement (Systems screen) - side by side · end to end
controls.desc: Puts the two springs in parallel or in series.
controls.tip: Side by side makes the pair stiffer; end to end makes it stretch more easily. Worth checking for yourself.

steps: On the Intro screen turn on all the checkboxes on the right.
Raise Applied Force and see whether Displacement keeps pace.
Double the Spring Constant and apply the same force.
Move to the Energy screen.
Note the energy at stretches of 0.1 · 0.2 · 0.3 m.
See whether the Energy Plot is a straight line or a curve.
On the Systems screen, try the two springs side by side and end to end.
gotchas: Force is proportional to the stretch but energy goes as the square. Twice the stretch is four times the energy.
Without the Values checkbox on, no numbers appear.
Displacement here means "how far it stretched". It does not mean the spring has moved somewhere.
Nothing moves in this sim. Springs that oscillate come in the next lesson (Masses and Springs).

masses-and-springs.summary: Hang a mass on a spring and let it oscillate. The aim is to find what sets the round trip time, which makes the stopwatch the most important tool here.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Hang masses on two springs and compare them.

screens.name: Vectors
screens.what: Shows velocity and acceleration as arrows.

screens.name: Energy
screens.what: Kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential and thermal energy as bars.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: Work out the mass of a weight whose value is hidden.

controls.name: Masses (drag from the rack on the left)
controls.desc: There are 50 g, 100 g and 250 g weights and a ? weight of unknown mass. Drag one onto a spring.
controls.tip: Once it is hanging, pull it down and let go to start it oscillating. Just hanging it on gives a small wobble that settles at the equilibrium.

controls.name: Damping (handle on the right)
controls.desc: Friction, like air resistance. Turn it up and the oscillation dies away.
controls.tip: To time the period, take it to 0. With friction it stops before you can count many round trips.

controls.name: Natural Length · Equilibrium Position · Movable Line (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Natural Length is where the spring ends with nothing on it, Equilibrium Position is where it settles with the mass, and Movable Line is a reference line you can put anywhere.
controls.tip: Leave Equilibrium Position on. You can see that the oscillation runs with that line at its centre.

controls.name: Spring Constant (handle above each spring)
controls.desc: Sets the stiffness of the spring, from Small to Large.
controls.tip: Set the two springs differently and hang the same mass on each. Watching them swing side by side shows the difference at once.

controls.name: Gravity (right) - Earth · Moon · Jupiter · Planet X · Custom
controls.desc: Changes the strength of gravity.
controls.tip: Switch to the Moon and the equilibrium position rises. But the round trip time does not change - do check that one.

controls.name: Stopwatch (top left)
controls.desc: Drag it out, then start and stop it.
controls.tip: The most important tool in this lesson. Timing a single round trip has too much error - time 10 and divide by 10.

controls.name: Energy bars (left of the Energy screen)
controls.desc: Five of them: KE · PEgrav · PEelas · Etherm · Etotal.
controls.tip: The same structure as the skate park in course 02, with one extra - elastic energy. There is a spring here.

controls.name: Speed setting and the step button (bottom)
controls.desc: Play it slowly or advance one frame at a time. Both are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: To catch the instant the speed reaches 0 at each end of the swing, run it slowly.

steps: Take Damping down to 0.
Turn on Natural Length and Equilibrium Position.
Hang the 100 g mass, pull it down a little and let it swing.
Time 10 round trips with the stopwatch and divide by 10.
Now pull it down a long way and time it the same way.
Change to the 250 g mass and time it again.
Raise the Spring Constant and time it again.
Change Gravity to Moon and check the round trip time.
gotchas: With Damping above 0 the swinging stops quickly and the period is hard to time.
Timing a single round trip carries too much error. Time 10 and divide.
The size of the swing does not change the period. Only the mass and the spring constant do.
Simply hanging a mass on does not start it oscillating. You have to pull it down and let go.

wave-on-a-string.summary: Shake the left end of a long string and send a wave down it. There is one screen and the controls are simple, so everything depends on what you fix your eyes on.

screens.name: (only one screen)
screens.what: This sim has a single screen. The black bar at the bottom carries no house button and no screen names.

controls.name: Manual · Oscillate · Pulse (top left)
controls.desc: Manual lets you shake the handle yourself, Oscillate shakes it continuously, and Pulse sends a single hump.
controls.tip: Start with Pulse. Following one hump with your eyes is the best way to see what a wave really does. Continuous waves come after.

controls.name: Fixed End · Loose End · No End (top right)
controls.desc: Sets how the right-hand end of the string is tied.
controls.tip: Fixed End comes back flipped; Loose End comes back the same way up. Do compare the two. No End gives no reflection at all.

controls.name: Damping (handle at the bottom)
controls.desc: Sets how much the wave dies away as it travels.
controls.tip: While you are after the rule, take it to 0. Otherwise the wave fades before it reaches the far end to reflect.

controls.name: Tension (handle at the bottom)
controls.desc: Sets how tight the string is.
controls.tip: Lower it and the wave gets slower. It shows you that the speed of a wave is set by the string, not by how hard you shake it.

controls.name: Reference Line (checkbox at the bottom right)
controls.desc: Puts a long horizontal reference line on screen. You can drag it about.
controls.tip: The key tool of this lesson. Use it to confirm that a single point on the string only travels up and down against that line.

controls.name: Rulers · Stopwatch (checkboxes at the bottom right)
controls.desc: Brings out horizontal and vertical rulers and a stopwatch.
controls.tip: Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next. Lay a ruler along the string to measure it.

controls.name: Restart String (bottom center)
controls.desc: Straightens the string and puts everything back to the start.
controls.tip: When the waves get tangled, press this first.

controls.name: Speed setting and the step button (bottom)
controls.desc: Play slowly or advance one frame at a time. Both are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: Step forward a frame at a time and watch a point on the reference line. That it moves only up and down becomes unmistakable.

steps: Set it to Pulse and take Damping down to 0.
Leave the end on Fixed End and send one pulse.
Turn on Reference Line and fix your eyes on one point of the string.
Use Slow Motion and the step button to check how that point moves.
Watch whether the pulse comes back flipped from the end.
Change the end to Loose End and watch again.
Switch to Oscillate and measure the wavelength with the Rulers.
Lower the Tension and watch the wave slow down.
gotchas: The string does not travel sideways. The only thing moving is the shape (the energy).
Damping is how fast the wave fades. Set high, the wave never reaches the end to reflect, so take it to 0.
Only Fixed End flips the reflected wave. Loose End comes back the same way up.
Shaking harder does not make the wave faster. Tension sets the speed.
With only one screen, the black bar at the bottom has no house button. Not a fault.

fourier-making-waves.summary: Build a waveform by adding sine waves together. The upper graph is the individual sine waves and the lower one is all of them added up.

screens.name: Discrete
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. "Discrete" means taken one at a time - you add the sine waves in one by one.

screens.name: Wave Game
screens.what: A game where you match a waveform you are given. Play it once the lesson is done.

screens.name: Wave Packet
screens.what: Adds a great many sine waves to build a short burst of wave. Much harder.

controls.name: Amplitude handles (the column on the left)
controls.desc: Set the size of each individual sine wave. They run n = 1, 2, 3… from the top, and the wavelength gets shorter as you go down.
controls.tip: Raise just one to begin with. Then two, then three, getting a feel for how the shape below goes out of shape.

controls.name: Waveform (right) - sinusoid · triangle · square · sawtooth · wave packet · custom
controls.desc: Choose the shape you want and the handles set themselves automatically.
controls.tip: Choose square and run the Harmonics number up and down. The heart of this lesson is in that single action.

controls.name: Harmonics (right)
controls.desc: Sets how many sine waves get added in.
controls.tip: Few leaves a lot of ripple; more gets closer to the target shape. Push it to the maximum and compare.

controls.name: Infinite Harmonics (checkbox at the bottom)
controls.desc: Draws the true shape you would get from adding infinitely many.
controls.tip: Leave it on while you raise the Harmonics. You can see straight away how close yours is getting to the real thing.

controls.name: Harmonics chart (top)
controls.desc: Shows the sine waves you are adding, one by one.
controls.tip: Look back and forth between the top and the bottom. How the individual waves up top combine down below is the whole sim.

controls.name: Sum chart (bottom)
controls.desc: The result of adding every sine wave together.
controls.tip: This is the product. Compare it against the target waveform.

controls.name: Measurement Tools - Wavelength · Period (bottom right)
controls.desc: Brings out a ruler for the wavelength or the period of an individual sine wave.
controls.tip: Measure the wavelength of n=1 and n=2. It is exactly half. That rule is how the sine waves are chosen.

controls.name: Equation · Series (right)
controls.desc: Writes what you have built as a formula, and lets you choose between sin and cos.
controls.tip: If the formula is heavy going, leave it on Hidden. The pictures alone are enough for this lesson.

steps: On the Discrete screen, raise only the first Amplitude handle.
Raise the second as well and watch the shape below go out of shape.
Choose square under Waveform.
Lower the Harmonics number and see the ripple that is left.
Push Harmonics to the maximum and watch it square up.
Turn on Infinite Harmonics and compare with yours.
Try sawtooth and triangle too.
gotchas: A finite number of sine waves never gives a perfect square wave. Ripple near the corners is normal.
This sim was built for high school and university. This lesson uses only the Discrete screen.
If the formula is heavy going, leave Equation on Hidden. The pictures are enough.

geometric-optics.summary: Watch how an image is formed by lenses and mirrors. Drag the object or the lens and the rays and the image follow immediately.

screens.name: Lens
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Convex and concave lenses.

screens.name: Mirror
screens.what: Concave, convex and flat mirrors. Almost the same rules as the lenses.

controls.name: The object (left, drag it about)
controls.desc: Choose between a pencil, a penguin, a star, an arrow and a light, and drag it to change its distance from the lens.
controls.tip: The main thing you do here. Drag it slowly from outside the focal point (F) to inside it. Where the real image gives way to a virtual image is the heart of this lesson.

controls.name: Rays (bottom left) - Marginal · Principal · Many · None
controls.desc: Chooses which rays to draw. Principal is the three representative rays used for drawing; Many is the real light spreading in all directions.
controls.tip: The most important switch in this lesson. Go from Principal to Many. Once you know there are not just three rays, the idea that "covering a lens cuts the image" falls apart.

controls.name: Focal Length · Radius of Curvature · Index of Refraction · Diameter (bottom)
controls.desc: Set the properties of the lens. Diameter is how big the lens is.
controls.tip: Try shrinking the Diameter. The image stays as it is but gets dimmer - which means a bigger lens gathers more light.

controls.name: Focal Points (F) · 2F Points (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Marks the focal points on either side of the lens and the points at twice that distance.
controls.tip: Leave them on. Where you put the object only means anything relative to the focal point, so with the focus hidden you cannot judge a thing.

controls.name: Virtual Image (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Draws the image that looks as though the light gathers there when it does not.
controls.tip: Pull the object inside the focal point and then tick it. This is what you are looking at when a magnifying glass enlarges text.

controls.name: Labels · Second Point · Guides (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Adds name tags, puts a second point on the object, and draws guide lines for the lens.
controls.tip: Labels is worth leaving on. It keeps you from mixing up the real image and the virtual image.

controls.name: Screen (when the object is set to Light)
controls.desc: Drag it to where the image forms and the image is thrown onto it.
controls.tip: A real image shows on the screen and a virtual image does not. It is the best way to feel the difference with your own hands.

steps: On the Lens screen turn on Focal Points (F) and Labels.
Set Rays to Principal and watch the three rays meet at one point.
Change Rays to Many and watch the light spread in every direction.
Drag the object nearer and further and watch the position and size of the image.
Pull the object inside the focal point and turn on Virtual Image.
Shrink the Diameter and watch the image get dimmer.
On the Mirror screen, do the same with a concave mirror.
gotchas: The three Principal rays are a trick to make the drawing easy. The real light is closer to what Many shows.
A virtual image will not show on a screen, because no light actually gathers there.
Cover part of the lens and the shape of the image is unchanged. It only gets dimmer.

blackbody-spectrum.summary: A sim where one handle is nearly all of it. Change the temperature of an object and a curve draws how much light comes out at each wavelength. With only one screen, the black bar at the bottom carries no screen names.

screens.name: (only one screen)
screens.what: This sim has a single screen. Change the temperature and watch how the curve moves.

controls.name: Blackbody Temperature (the vertical handle on the right)
controls.desc: Sets the temperature of the object. The one main control here.
controls.tip: Raise it slowly and watch which way the peak of the curve moves. Jump it up all at once and you miss the change happening.

controls.name: The wavelength scale (horizontal axis)
controls.desc: From the left it is divided by colour into X-Ray · Ultraviolet · Visible · Infrared.
controls.tip: Look at how narrow the visible band is. It shows at a glance that what our eyes can see is a very small slice of the whole.

controls.name: Real object buttons (right) - Earth · Light Bulb · Sun · Sirius A
controls.desc: Loads the temperature of a real object.
controls.tip: Press all four in turn and note the temperature and where the peak is. The Earth has its peak in the infrared, so you cannot see it.

controls.name: Graph Values · Labels (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Puts values on the curve and names on the bands.
controls.tip: Turn them on when you want to read the peak wavelength exactly.

controls.name: Intensity (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Shows the total intensity as a number. It is the area under the curve.
controls.tip: Double the temperature and compare the values. Not twice - sixteen times.

controls.name: The coloured square (top right)
controls.desc: Tells you what colour an object at that temperature looks.
controls.tip: The curve alone does not give you a feel for it. Watch this little square alongside and "red → white → blue" lands immediately.

controls.name: The R · G · B readouts (under the visible band)
controls.desc: Show how much of each of the three colours is coming out.
controls.tip: When all three come out about equally, the object looks white. The Sun is around there.

steps: Take the temperature down to about 3000 K and see where the peak is.
Raise it slowly and watch which way the peak goes.
Find the temperature that brings the peak into the Visible band.
Turn on Intensity, double the temperature and compare the values.
Press Earth · Light Bulb · Sun · Sirius A in turn.
Check the colour at each temperature with the coloured square at the top right.
gotchas: Blue is hotter than red. The opposite of the red and blue on a tap.
Double the temperature and the intensity goes to sixteen times. It goes as the fourth power.
At low temperatures the curve looks as though it is flat on the floor. The vertical scale rescales itself; the value is not 0.
The curve is continuous, with no breaks - unlike the hydrogen spectrum in course 05, which was a few separate lines.
With only one screen, the black bar at the bottom has no house button.

photoelectric-effect.summary: Shine light on a metal and see whether electrons fly out. There are only two handles - Intensity and Wavelength.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Choose a metal, shine light on it and watch the current.

screens.name: Experiment
screens.what: Measure the threshold of an unknown Mystery metal and work out what it is.

screens.name: Energy
screens.what: Shows how much energy the electrons come out with.

controls.name: Intensity - handle at the top
controls.desc: Sets the intensity of the light. It corresponds to the number of photons.
controls.tip: This is the handle that settles ② in this lesson. Do see for yourself that at a long wavelength the current stays 0 even at full intensity.

controls.name: Wavelength - handle at the top
controls.desc: Sets the wavelength of the light. UV is to the left and IR to the right. It settles the energy of one photon.
controls.tip: Fix the intensity and lower only this, slowly. The point where the current suddenly starts to flow is that metal's threshold.

controls.name: The metal chooser (left) - a combo box with no label above it
controls.desc: Choose between Sodium, Copper, Calcium, Platinum, Zinc and Mystery. The box itself carries no heading; it shows the name of the metal you have picked.
controls.tip: Start with Sodium. It has the lowest threshold, so visible light is enough to get electrons out. Platinum takes ultraviolet.

controls.name: Current - the meter on the right
controls.desc: The current made by the electrons that fly out, in μA.
controls.tip: Where the answer appears in this sim. A reading of 0 means not one electron came out.

controls.name: Show Electrons - checkbox at the bottom
controls.desc: Makes the escaping electrons visible.
controls.tip: Leave it on. Watching the grains fly stays with you far better than a number for the current.

controls.name: Highest Energy Only
controls.desc: Picks out only the fastest electrons to show.
controls.tip: Turn it on once you know the electrons come out at a range of speeds. How far past the threshold you are sets the maximum energy.

controls.name: Representation chooser (two pictures, no words - grounded / circuit)
controls.desc: Chooses whether the apparatus is drawn as a grounded setup or as a circuit diagram. The two buttons carry pictures only.
controls.tip: The result is the same either way. If circuits are familiar to you, the circuit picture is easier to follow.

controls.name: Pause and step buttons (bottom)
controls.desc: Stop the action or advance a frame at a time. Both are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: Use them when you want to catch the instant an electron flies off.

steps: Set the metal to Sodium and put the wavelength long, over toward IR.
Push Intensity to maximum and confirm that Current reads 0.
Leaving the intensity alone, bring Wavelength down slowly toward UV.
Write down the threshold wavelength at which the current starts to flow.
Just past the threshold, turn the intensity down and see whether electrons still come.
Change the metal to Copper and Platinum and compare the thresholds.
On the Energy screen, see what the wavelength changes and what the intensity changes.
gotchas: At a wavelength longer than the threshold, no intensity at all gets a single electron out. Not a fault.
Intensity sets the number of electrons; wavelength sets the energy of each one. Mix the two and you reach no conclusion.
The threshold is different for every metal. Sodium is low, platinum is high.
This sim has three screens. Start on Intro.

quantum-wave-interference.summary: Fire light or particles at a barrier with two slits and see what pattern piles up on the screen behind. Taking the intensity very low so they go one at a time is the key move in this lesson.

screens.name: Experiment
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Slit settings and intensity are both free to change.

screens.name: High Intensity
screens.what: Fire the light hard and see the whole pattern at once.

screens.name: Single Particles
screens.what: A screen built around sending the particles one at a time.

controls.name: Source Intensity (left)
controls.desc: Sets how much you fire. Max is the top of the range.
controls.tip: The most important handle in this lesson. See the pattern at maximum, then take it very low to send them one at a time. That contrast is the whole thing.

controls.name: Slit Configuration (middle)
controls.desc: Both Open · Cover Left · Cover Right, along with the detector settings.
controls.tip: Work through Both Open → Cover Left → Cover Right. Cover one and the stripes vanish, leaving a single smear.

controls.name: Detector Left · Right · Both (watching which slit)
controls.desc: Switches on the apparatus that checks which slit the particle went through.
controls.tip: The strangest part of this sim. Switch it on and the stripes vanish. The act of looking changes the result.

controls.name: Detection mode - Intensity · Hits
controls.desc: Chooses whether the screen shows brightness or a dot where each one landed. The pair of buttons has no heading of its own.
controls.tip: When you send them one at a time, use Hits. You get to watch the dots arrive one by one and the pattern build up.

controls.name: Particle chooser (bottom left)
controls.desc: Choose between Photons, Electrons, Neutrons and Helium Atoms. The group carries no heading; each button shows its own name.
controls.tip: Switch to Electrons. Matter, not light, makes the same pattern - which makes this lesson's conclusion far stronger.

controls.name: Wavelength (left)
controls.desc: Sets the wavelength of the light you fire.
controls.tip: Shorten it and the stripes pack closer together. Evidence of wave-like behaviour.

controls.name: Slit Separation · Barrier-Screen Distance
controls.desc: Set the distance between the two slits and the distance to the screen.
controls.tip: Narrow the separation and the pattern spreads wider. Basic wave behaviour.

controls.name: The clear and snapshot buttons (by the screen)
controls.desc: Wipe the dots that have piled up, or save the current state. Both are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: When you change conditions to compare, wipe the screen first. Otherwise the dots from the last run are mixed in.

controls.name: Particle Speed (bottom)
controls.desc: Sets how fast the run goes.
controls.tip: Sending them one at a time takes a while for a pattern to build. Set it fast and wait.

steps: Check the particle chooser at the bottom left is on Photons and set the intensity to Max.
On Both Open, watch the stripes appear.
Switch to Cover Left and Cover Right and watch one smear remain.
Go back to Both Open and take the intensity very low.
Change the detection mode to Hits, run it fast and leave it a long while.
Watch the stripes appear as the dots pile up.
Change the particle chooser to Electrons and do the same again.
Turn on Detector Left and see what happens to the pattern.
gotchas: Sent one at a time, the first few land anywhere at all. Do not give up because no pattern shows - leave it running.
Adding the two covered-slit smears together does not make the stripes. That is exactly what is strange about it.
Turn a Detector on and the pattern goes. Not a fault - that is the very result the sim is here to show.
Wipe the screen before you change conditions.
This sim was built at university level. The Experiment screen alone is enough for this lesson.

build-an-atom.summary: Build an atom yourself by dragging protons, neutrons and electrons out of their buckets.

screens.name: Atom
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Add and remove particles and watch what moves the element, the charge and the mass number.

screens.name: Symbol
screens.what: The same building, with the element symbol shown large on the right. The number above is the mass number, below is the proton count, and top right is the charge.

screens.name: Game
screens.what: A four-level check: identify the element, calculate mass and charge, fill in the symbol, and a mixed review.

controls.name: The Protons · Neutrons · Electrons buckets (bottom centre)
controls.desc: Drag a particle out of a bucket and into the atom. Drag it back to the bucket to take it out again.
controls.tip: The one key action in this sim. Add one kind at a time and watch what changes on screen. Add all three at once and you will not know what caused what.

controls.name: Model - Shells · Cloud (top left)
controls.desc: Radio buttons for how the electrons are drawn. Shells is the old picture with lines; Cloud is the modern one, blurred and spread out.
controls.tip: Not one value changes. Only the picture changes. Lesson 3 takes up which of them is closer to reality.

controls.name: Element Name (checkbox)
controls.desc: Puts the name of the element in words under the atom.
controls.tip: Leave it on. Far quicker than hunting for the cell in the periodic table with your eyes.

controls.name: Neutral Atom or Ion (checkbox)
controls.desc: Tells you it is an ion when the electron and proton counts do not match, and a neutral atom when they do.
controls.tip: Add and remove electrons while watching this readout and it becomes obvious that electrons change the charge, never the element.

controls.name: Nuclear Stability (checkbox)
controls.desc: Tells you whether the combination is one a nucleus can hold. When it is unstable the nucleus picture shakes.
controls.tip: Keep adding neutrons. At some point it tips over into unstable. A trailer for lesson 4 (Build a Nucleus).

controls.name: Periodic Table (collapsible box, top right)
controls.desc: The periodic table, with the cell for the element you have built lit up.
controls.tip: You cannot press a cell to choose an element. It only reports - the element changes when you add protons.

controls.name: Net Charge · Mass Number (collapsible boxes, bottom right)
controls.desc: Net Charge is the difference between protons and electrons; Mass Number is protons plus neutrons.
controls.tip: Open both at once and add particles. The table of which particle moves which number draws itself.

steps: Tick Element Name and Neutral Atom or Ion first.
Put in one proton only and check the element name.
Add one neutron and see that the name does not change.
Add one more proton and see that this time it does.
Take one electron away and watch for the ion readout.
Turn on Nuclear Stability and keep adding neutrons.
gotchas: The periodic table cells do nothing when pressed. They only report the result.
The mass number does not count electrons, because an electron is far too light to matter.
You do not have to place a particle precisely. Drop it nearby and it finds its own place.
This sim has three screens. The lesson opens only the Atom screen.

rutherford-scattering.summary: Fire alpha particles at an atom and see how they bounce. The two screens are the old model and the new one, so going back and forth to compare them is the whole sim.

screens.name: Rutherford Atom
screens.what: The model with the mass gathered into one point at the centre. Protons and Neutrons handles are on the right.

screens.name: Plum Pudding Atom
screens.what: The old model, with the positive charge spread out. There is no atom panel - there is nothing to change. Worth starting here.

controls.name: The gun (bottom centre)
controls.desc: Press it and alpha particles fire continuously. Press again to stop.
controls.tip: Leave it on and wait. Big bounces are rare, so turning it off after a few seconds means you never see one.

controls.name: Alpha Particle - Energy (right)
controls.desc: Sets the speed of the alpha particles, from min to max.
controls.tip: Slower bends more sharply, because going past fast leaves no time to be pushed. Try both ends to find the rule.

controls.name: Traces (checkbox)
controls.desc: Leaves the path of each alpha particle drawn as a line.
controls.tip: Do turn this on. With it off the particles flash past and you cannot tell what happened. The single most important switch here.

controls.name: Atom - Protons · Neutrons (right, Rutherford screen only)
controls.desc: Changes the number of particles in the nucleus. Protons run 20-100, neutrons up to 150.
controls.tip: Change only the protons. The bouncing gets stronger because of the charge, not the weight. Adding neutrons barely changes it.

controls.name: Legend (top right)
controls.desc: Tells you what each dot on screen is - alpha particle, nucleus, electron energy level, alpha particle trace.
controls.tip: Open it once at the start. Mix up the yellow dots and the red ones and you will see nothing at all.

controls.name: The scale readout (top of the screen)
controls.desc: Tells you the size you are looking at, in m (atomic scale) or m (nuclear scale).
controls.tip: Read the numbers once. Atomic scale and nuclear scale differ by a factor of a hundred thousand. The nucleus is drawn big on screen; it is nothing like that in reality.

steps: Open the Plum Pudding Atom screen first.
Turn on Traces, switch the gun on and leave it a while.
Move to the Rutherford Atom screen and fire under the same conditions.
Wait until a big bounce happens.
Take Protons from 20 to 100 and watch how the bouncing changes.
Drop Energy to minimum and fire again.
gotchas: Big bounces are rare. Do not watch for a few seconds and conclude "it does not bounce" - the rarity is half the conclusion.
The nucleus on screen is drawn far larger than it really is. At true scale it would not be a visible dot.
The plum pudding screen has no atom panel. Not a fault - that model has no nucleus.
Adding neutrons barely changes the bouncing. What makes a bounce is charge, not weight.

models-of-the-hydrogen-atom.summary: Shine light into a hydrogen atom and look at the light that comes out with a spectrometer. The switch at the top left moves between Experiment (you cannot see inside) and Model (you can), and the point is to work out which model matches reality.

screens.name: Spectra
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. All six models are available.

screens.name: Energy Levels
screens.what: Only the three quantum models (Bohr, de Broglie, Schrödinger), but with the Electron Energy Level staircase added on the right.

controls.name: The Experiment / Model switch (top left)
controls.desc: On Experiment the inside of the box is hidden behind a ?. Slide it to Model and you can see in and pick a model.
controls.tip: Do the experiment first. Looking at the answer first makes the whole thing pointless. Write down the experimental result, then try the models against it.

controls.name: Model chooser (left)
controls.desc: Under Classical are Billiard Ball, Plum Pudding and Classical Solar System; under Quantum are Bohr, de Broglie and Schrödinger.
controls.tip: They are laid out top to bottom in historical order. Work down and find where they start matching the experiment.

controls.name: The light box - White · Monochromatic (bottom left)
controls.desc: White fires every colour at once; Monochromatic fires a single wavelength, and brings out a wavelength handle.
controls.tip: See the whole picture with white, then check one at a time with monochromatic. On monochromatic only the exactly right wavelength gets a response.

controls.name: Spectrometer (bottom centre)
controls.desc: Counts the light that comes out by wavelength and stacks it as bars. Along the bottom is wavelength (nm), divided into UV, Visible and IR.
controls.tip: Results take time to build up. Give it a few seconds before the lines show. Do not switch models the moment nothing appears.

controls.name: Transitions (bottom left, the button under the light box - it opens a window)
controls.desc: A list of the steps an electron can move between, written as 1 ↔ 2, 2 ↔ 3 and so on. It appears from Bohr onward; the earlier models have no such button at all.
controls.tip: Read the numbers inside - they tell you which step an electron can move to from which.

controls.name: Speed - Fast · Normal · Slow (bottom)
controls.desc: How fast the simulation runs.
controls.tip: To watch a single event of an electron jumping and spitting out light, set it to Slow. At normal speed it is over in an instant.

controls.name: Electron Energy Level (right of the Energy Levels screen)
controls.desc: Draws the steps from n = 1 to 6, showing which step the electron is on now.
controls.tip: Notice that the gaps narrow as you go up. That is why transitions between the high steps carry little energy and come out at long wavelengths, in the infrared.

steps: Leave the switch on Experiment and fire White light.
Count and note how many lines appear in the spectrometer.
Move the switch to Model and work down from Billiard Ball.
Find which model first gives the same lines as the experiment.
Change the light to Monochromatic and move the wavelength to find where it responds.
Drop the speed to Slow and watch the moment an electron jumps.
gotchas: Results take time to build up in the spectrometer. Nothing appearing straight away is not a fault.
Choose the Classical Solar System model and the electron spirals into the nucleus, so the sim looks as though it has stopped. That is precisely the evidence that the model is wrong.
This sim was built for high school. Grasping that there are only a few steps is enough.

build-a-nucleus.summary: Change only the number of protons and neutrons and see which nuclei hold together and which fall apart. Press a decay button and the nucleus really does break.

screens.name: Decay
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. You can go up to 94 protons and 146 neutrons.

screens.name: Chart Intro
screens.what: A nuclide chart with Neutron Number across and Proton Number up. This screen only goes to 10 protons and 12 neutrons.

controls.name: Protons · Neutrons (arrows at the bottom left)
controls.desc: Up and down arrows change the counts one at a time, and particles attach to or leave the nucleus.
controls.tip: Change one of them only. Hold the protons and raise the neutrons and you walk through the isotopes of one element - the proper way to use this sim.

controls.name: Half-life (the scale at the top left)
controls.desc: Shows how long the nucleus you have built survives, on a log scale from 10⁻²⁴ to 10²⁴ seconds. Stable nuclei sit off the scale, and combinations nobody has measured read Unknown.
controls.tip: The scale is logarithmic. One step is a thousand times. A small shift along it is an enormous difference.

controls.name: Available Decays (right)
controls.desc: The decays this nucleus can do, as buttons - α decay · β⁻ decay · β⁺ decay · Proton emission · Neutron emission. Press one and it really decays.
controls.tip: Note the proton and neutron counts before you press. Comparing afterwards builds the table of what each decay changes, for free.

controls.name: Symbol (collapsible box on the right)
controls.desc: Shows the element symbol with the mass number and the proton count.
controls.tip: Leave it open. It is the fastest place to see whether the element changed after a decay.

controls.name: The less stable / more stable scale
controls.desc: An arrow telling you whether this nucleus is on the stable side.
controls.tip: Move the neutrons one at a time and watch the arrow. You get a feel for which way you have to go to become stable.

controls.name: Electron Cloud (checkbox)
controls.desc: Draws the electron cloud around the nucleus.
controls.tip: The nucleus is the star of this sim. Leaving the cloud off makes it easier to watch.

controls.name: Partial Nuclide Chart · Full Chart · Magic Numbers (Chart Intro screen)
controls.desc: Choose a narrow or a wide view of the nuclide chart, and turn on Magic Numbers to mark the unusually stable rows.
controls.tip: Take the wide view with Full Chart and you can see the stable nuclei forming a diagonal band. Decay is, in the end, an attempt to get inside that band.

steps: Set 6 protons and 6 neutrons (carbon-12) and look at the half-life.
Take the neutrons alone up to 8 (carbon-14) and see how the half-life changes.
Open the Symbol box and note the proton and neutron counts.
Press a button under Available Decays to decay it, and note the numbers again.
Keep raising the neutrons until you reach Unknown.
On the Chart Intro screen turn on Full Chart and Magic Numbers and look at the shape of the band.
gotchas: The half-life scale is logarithmic. One step is a thousand times.
Unknown is not a fault. It means nobody has yet made or measured that combination.
If a decay changes the proton count, it changes the element. Do check the name tag.
The Chart Intro screen only goes to 10 protons and 12 neutrons. Heavy nuclei can only be built on the Decay screen.
β⁻ and β⁺ are different decays. The minus turns a neutron into a proton; the plus turns a proton into a neutron.

alpha-decay.summary: The three screens run one atom → several → a great many, so going through them in order is itself the design of this sim.

screens.name: Single Atom
screens.what: Watch when one atom decays. It is different every time. An energy diagram is attached below.

screens.name: Multiple Atoms
screens.what: Put down several atoms and watch them decay one by one. A tendency starts to show.

screens.name: Decay Rate
screens.what: Draws the percentage remaining of a great many atoms as a curve. You get a smooth exponential.

controls.name: Add Atom
controls.desc: Puts down one polonium-211 atom. Once it decays you can press again for a fresh one.
controls.tip: Repeat it more than ten times. Once or twice will not show you "different every time", and that repetition is the heart of this lesson.

controls.name: Decay Time
controls.desc: Prints, in seconds, how long this atom took to decay.
controls.tip: Write down just five of them on paper. Seeing the numbers all over the place is the point.

controls.name: Half-life handle
controls.desc: Changes the half-life. The Time Scale below runs logarithmically from ms to 10⁹ yr.
controls.tip: A short half-life ends each run quickly, which is good for repeating. Keep it short while you are looking for the rule.

controls.name: Isotope - Polonium-211 · Custom
controls.desc: Choose a real isotope or build your own. Custom lets you set the protons and neutrons freely.
controls.tip: Leave it on Polonium-211 to start with. Real values mean the nuclear equation later matches a textbook exactly.

controls.name: Nuclear Equation
controls.desc: Writes the decay as a formula: ²¹¹Po → ²⁰⁷Pb + ⁴He. The upper number is the mass number, the lower one the proton count.
controls.tip: Add up the top and bottom numbers separately. 211 = 207 + 4, 84 = 82 + 2. Both sides always match - nothing is lost and nothing is created.

controls.name: Energy Diagram (below, on the Single Atom screen)
controls.desc: Distance across, Energy up. The Alpha Particle Energy is lower than the Potential Energy wall, and it gets out anyway.
controls.tip: This is tunnelling. It passes through a wall it cannot climb, so when it will pass can only be spoken of as a probability. The real reason decay is unruly.

controls.name: Labels · Stopwatch (Multiple Atoms screen)
controls.desc: Puts a name tag on each atom, and brings out a stopwatch.
controls.tip: Turn Labels on and you can see at a glance which atoms are still polonium and which have already become lead.

controls.name: Data Probe (Decay Rate screen)
controls.desc: Drag it onto the curve and it reads the Isotope Remaining (%) at that moment.
controls.tip: Put it on Half-lives 1, 2 and 3 in turn. It reads exactly 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5.

controls.name: Normal · Slow (speed)
controls.desc: How fast the simulation runs.
controls.tip: To catch the moment of a decay, use Slow.

steps: On the Single Atom screen press Add Atom to put an atom down.
Note the Decay Time, and repeat the whole thing more than ten times.
Open the Nuclear Equation and check that the top and bottom numbers balance.
On the Energy Diagram, see the alpha particle shut inside the wall.
On the Multiple Atoms screen put down several atoms and turn on Labels.
On the Decay Rate screen look at the curve and read values off with the Data Probe.
gotchas: When one atom decays cannot be predicted. The point is to run it several times and see the times come out all over the place.
Atoms do not age. Waiting a long time does not bring one closer to its turn.
Half-lives and Half-life are different things. The first is a count, the second is the length of one.
The energy diagram is only on the Single Atom screen. You will not find it on the others.

beta-decay.summary: The controls are almost identical to the alpha decay sim, and the three screens run in the same order. The only difference is what flies out and what happens to the proton count, so if you have done lesson 5 you can concentrate on that difference alone.

screens.name: Single Atom
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Watch one tritium (³H) or carbon-14 atom decay.

screens.name: Multiple Atoms
screens.what: Put down several atoms and watch them decay one by one.

screens.name: Decay Rate
screens.what: The percentage-remaining curve. Compare it against alpha decay and see whether it is the same shape.

controls.name: Isotope - Hydrogen-3 · Carbon-14 · Custom
controls.desc: Choose tritium (³H), carbon-14, or a nucleus you build yourself.
controls.tip: Do try Carbon-14. It is the nucleus you built in lesson 4 (Build a Nucleus), and the very one used for dating.

controls.name: Protons · Neutrons
controls.desc: The proton and neutron counts of the current nucleus.
controls.tip: The most important readout in this sim. Note both numbers before and after the decay - you get neutrons −1, protons +1.

controls.name: Nuclear Equation
controls.desc: Written out as ³H → ³He + e⁻.
controls.tip: Check that the upper number (the mass number) does not change. In alpha decay it dropped by 4; here it holds. That is the biggest difference between the two decays.

controls.name: Half-life handle
controls.desc: Changes the half-life. The Time Scale below runs from ms to 10⁹ yr.
controls.tip: The real half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years. Find roughly where that sits on the scale.

controls.name: Labels · Stopwatch (Multiple Atoms screen)
controls.desc: Puts a name tag on each atom and times them.
controls.tip: Turn Labels on and you can watch ³H turn into ³He in words. The clearest possible demonstration that the element changes.

controls.name: Data Probe (Decay Rate screen)
controls.desc: Reads the percentage remaining off the curve.
controls.tip: Compare against the values you read for alpha decay. They are the same. Different kinds of decay, one rule of half-life.

steps: On the Single Atom screen put an atom down and note Protons and Neutrons.
Wait for it to decay, then note both numbers again and compare.
Open the Nuclear Equation and check the mass number is unchanged.
Change Isotope to Carbon-14 and do the same.
On the Multiple Atoms screen turn on Labels and watch the element change.
Compare the curve on the Decay Rate screen against lesson 5.
gotchas: The electron that flies out did not come from the electron shells. It is made inside the nucleus at the instant of decay.
In β⁻ decay the mass number does not change. One neutron turned into one proton, so the total holds.
The layout is the same as alpha decay, which is easy to confuse. If the starting atom is ³H you are here; if it is ²¹¹Po you are in the alpha sim.
Alpha Particle may still appear in the legend. The two sims share components; no alpha particle comes out of beta decay.

quantum-coin-toss.summary: The screen is split down the middle: an ordinary coin on the left, a quantum coin on the right. Doing the same thing on both sides and comparing the results is the whole of this sim.

screens.name: Coins
