screens.what: This sim has a single screen, split left and right to handle the two kinds of coin side by side.

controls.name: Coin to Prepare (top left)
controls.desc: The settings for the ordinary coin. Initial Orientation picks the starting face - the two buttons show the faces as pictures, with no words on them.
controls.tip: An ordinary coin has a state before you throw it. What you set here is that state.

controls.name: Coin Bias (State) - handle on the left
controls.desc: Sets the probability of the first face. 0.5 is fifty-fifty.
controls.tip: Set the same probability on both sides before comparing. With different probabilities there is nothing to compare.

controls.name: State to Prepare (top right)
controls.desc: The quantum coin side. The state is written with two values, α and β. Square each of them to get a probability.
controls.tip: Set α = β = 0.707 for a fifty-fifty probability (0.707² ≈ 0.5). Start from those values.

controls.name: Hide · Flip · Flip and Reveal (ordinary coin side)
controls.desc: Hide the coin, flip it, or flip and reveal it.
controls.tip: The Hide state is the key picture of this lesson - already settled, and I cannot see it.

controls.name: Observe · Reprepare · Reprepare and Observe (quantum coin side)
controls.desc: Observe settles the state into one value; Reprepare puts it back into superposition.
controls.tip: Press Reprepare and Observe several times over. You can see it settled anew each time.

controls.name: Multiple Coin Measurements (bottom)
controls.desc: Measures N coins at once, up to 100.
controls.tip: The decisive experiment of this lesson. Measure 100 on each side and see whether the results alone let you tell them apart - they do not.

controls.name: New Coin (bottom left)
controls.desc: Puts everything back to the start.
controls.tip: When the settings get tangled, press this first.

steps: On the Classical Coin side, do Flip and Reveal several times.
Set Coin Bias (State) to 0.5.
On the Quantum "Coin" side, set α and β to 0.707 each.
Press Observe several times and look at the results.
Under Multiple Coin Measurements set N = 100 and measure both sides.
Compare the two results and see whether you can tell them apart.
Repeat Reprepare and Observe and watch it settle anew each time.
gotchas: The results alone cannot tell the two coins apart. That is not a failure; it is the conclusion of this sim.
α and β are not probabilities but values that become probabilities when squared. 0.707² ≈ 0.5.
Once you Observe the quantum coin it is fixed at that value. Press Reprepare to put it back into superposition.
This sim was built at university level. You can follow it from the two probabilities alone, without the algebra of α and β.

quantum-measurement.summary: Shows quantum measurement in four different ways. It opens with the same coin story as the previous lesson, then moves on to photons and spin.

screens.name: Coins
screens.what: The same material as the previous lesson (Quantum Coin Toss). Worth one more look if any of it did not land.

screens.name: Photons
screens.what: The key screen for this lesson. Measurement handled through the polarization of light.

screens.name: Spin
screens.what: The same story told with the spin of an electron. Measuring devices can be put in a row.

screens.name: Bloch Sphere
screens.what: Draws a quantum state as a point on a ball. The hardest screen.

controls.name: Single Photon · Many Photons (top of the Photons screen)
controls.desc: Choose whether to send photons one at a time or in numbers.
controls.tip: Start with Single Photon. This lesson only works once you have seen one grain go one way whole. Proportions come after.

controls.name: Photon Polarization Angle (bottom left)
controls.desc: Choose between Vertical (V), Horizontal (H), 45°, Unpolarized and Custom.
controls.tip: The main control here. Go from Vertical to 45°. On vertical the result is settled; at 45° it cannot be predicted.

controls.name: Behavior - Classical · Quantum (middle)
controls.desc: Choose whether light is handled as a wave or as grains.
controls.tip: The best contrast in this lesson. Classical divides the intensity and sends both ways; Quantum sends it whole, one way.

controls.name: Polarizing Beam Splitter (middle)
controls.desc: Splits the incoming light into a vertical component and a horizontal component and sends them to different detectors.
controls.tip: This is the "measuring device". The moment a photon passes it, its polarization is settled into one of the two.

controls.name: Polarization Detectors (middle - vertical above, horizontal below)
controls.desc: Count the photons that arrive. The difference between the two counts gives the average polarization.
controls.tip: At 45° the two counts come out close together. Each one is unruly and the whole is even.

controls.name: Vector Representation · Expectation Value · Decimal Values (right)
controls.desc: Show the result as an arrow, as an expectation value, and as numbers.
controls.tip: If the algebra is heavy going, leave only Decimal Values on. The proportions alone are enough for this lesson.

controls.name: Chaining measuring devices (Spin screen)
controls.desc: Put several measuring devices in a row, each at its own angle.
controls.tip: Try vertical → horizontal → vertical. The first vertical result being erased is the most startling thing in this sim.

controls.name: Speed setting and the step button (bottom)
controls.desc: Play slowly or advance one frame at a time. Both are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: To watch one photon pass the splitter, run it slowly.

steps: On the Coins screen, go over the previous lesson's material again.
Move to the Photons screen and set the angle to Vertical (V).
Send them one at a time on Single Photon and see whether it always goes the same way.
Change the angle to 45° and watch it become unpredictable.
Switch to Many Photons and check the split is even.
Switch Behavior between Classical and Quantum and compare.
On the Spin screen put devices in a row at different angles.
gotchas: A single photon is not divided in half. It goes one way whole - check it under Quantum behavior.
There are four screens and they get harder as you go. Coins → Photons is enough for this lesson.
The Bloch Sphere screen is university level. Have a look round it if you are curious.

quantum-bound-states.summary: Confine an electron in a box and see what energies it can have. The upper graph is the energy staircase and the lower one is the wave shape, so the trick is to watch both together.

screens.name: One Well
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. You can change the confining shape in several ways.

screens.name: Two Wells
screens.what: Two wells, with the electron moving between them. Much harder.

screens.name: Many Wells
screens.what: Wells in a row. Closer to the situation of an electron in a solid.

controls.name: The confining-shape chooser (top right - a combo box with no heading, showing the current shape)
controls.desc: Choose between Infinite Square, Finite Square, Harmonic Oscillator, Coulomb and others.
controls.tip: Start on Infinite Square, the simplest box. Coulomb is the situation of the hydrogen atom from course 05.

controls.name: The energy staircase (the horizontal lines in the upper graph)
controls.desc: The energies the electron can have. Press a line to select that state.
controls.tip: The answer to this lesson is here. The gaps between the lines are empty - those energies are impossible.

controls.name: The width and depth handles (small handles on the graph)
controls.desc: Drag to change the width and depth of the box. The readout beside each says width = … nm or depth = … eV.
controls.tip: The key action in this lesson. Narrow the width and the steps spread apart; widen it and they pack together. Why quantum is invisible in daily life comes out of this.

controls.name: Quantum State Graph (right) - Probability Density · Wave Function
controls.desc: Choose whether the lower graph shows the probability density or the wave function.
controls.tip: Probability Density is the easier one to read. It shows you where the electron is likely to be found.

controls.name: Energy Level (right)
controls.desc: Choose between E₁ · E₂ · E₃ and so on. Pressing a line in the upper graph does the same thing.
controls.tip: Work up from E₁ and watch the number of humps rise by one each time. The same shapes as the guitar string harmonics in course 03.

controls.name: Mass (right)
controls.desc: Changes the mass of the confined particle, in units of the electron mass.
controls.tip: Heavier packs the steps closer together. Much the same effect as widening the box - heavy things do not show quantum effects.

controls.name: Values · Magnifier · Reference Line (bottom left)
controls.desc: Put values on screen as numbers, and bring out a magnifier and a reference line.
controls.tip: Turn on Values and you can read each step's energy as a number. Good for measuring how far the gaps open up.

controls.name: Hide-curve, restart and pause buttons
controls.desc: Hide a graph, or wind the time back and stop it. All are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: If the wave rippling with time is distracting, stop it with the pause button and look at the shape alone.

steps: Check the confining shape is Infinite Square.
Look at the horizontal lines in the upper graph and the empty space between them.
Select E₁ · E₂ · E₃ in turn and count the humps in the wave.
Switch to Probability Density and look at where it is likely to be found.
Drag the width handle to narrow the box and watch the step spacing.
Widen the box and watch the steps pack together.
Change the shape to Coulomb for the situation of the hydrogen atom.
gotchas: The energies between the steps cannot be had. The empty space is the answer to this lesson.
The narrower the box, the wider the step spacing. It can feel backwards.
At E₂ the electron is never found at the middle of the box. Not an error.
The wave ripples with time. To look at the shape alone, stop it with the pause button.
This sim was built at university level. Grasping that there are steps and that narrowing spreads them is enough.

gravity-and-orbits.summary: Set up pairs like a star and a planet, or the Earth and the Moon, and watch how an orbit holds itself together. Being able to switch gravity on and off is the key device in this sim.

screens.name: Model
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Drawn at exaggerated sizes so you can see it.

screens.name: To Scale
screens.what: Drawn at true proportions. The bodies shrink below a dot and almost vanish - which is itself the thing to learn.

controls.name: The system chooser (bottom)
controls.desc: Choose between a star and planet, a star with planet and moon, the Earth and Moon, and the Earth with a satellite. The buttons are pictures of the bodies.
controls.tip: Start with the star and planet. With only two of them, what is happening is at its clearest.

controls.name: Gravity - on · off (top right)
controls.desc: Switches gravity on and off. Switch it off and the bodies fly off straight.
controls.tip: The most important button in this sim. Press it while it is orbiting - you understand what an orbit is in one go.

controls.name: Velocity · Path · Grid (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Turn on the velocity arrows, the trail, and the background grid.
controls.tip: Turn on all three. Path especially - without it the shape of the orbit leaves no trace in your eye.

controls.name: The velocity arrow (the V mark on a body)
controls.desc: Drag the tip of the arrow to change the size and direction of the velocity.
controls.tip: The main action here. Nudge it down and up and hunt for the point where the orbit falls apart.

controls.name: Mass handles (bottom right)
controls.desc: Change Star Mass · Planet Mass · Moon Mass · Satellite Mass separately.
controls.tip: Make the star heavier and it pulls harder, so the orbit shrinks. Compare what happens at the same speed.

controls.name: Return Objects · Clear (top left and below)
controls.desc: Put the bodies back where they started, or wipe the path that has been drawn.
controls.tip: When you run several experiments, Clear the trail before each one. Otherwise the lines tangle.

controls.name: Zoom (top left)
controls.desc: Zooms the view in and out.
controls.tip: If a body flies off, zoom out and chase it. Seeing how far it gets is entertaining in itself.

controls.name: Fast · Normal · Slow (bottom)
controls.desc: The playback speed of the simulation.
controls.tip: If one circuit takes a long time, use Fast. To catch the moment you switch gravity off, use Slow.

steps: On the Model screen choose the star and planet.
Turn on Velocity · Path · Grid.
Press play and let it go round a few times.
Switch Gravity to off and see what happens.
Press Return Objects, then shrink the velocity arrow.
Now make the velocity much larger.
Change the Star Mass and see how the orbit changes.
Open the To Scale screen once.
gotchas: The sizes and distances on screen are exaggerated. For the true proportions, look at the To Scale screen.
The velocity arrow always points along the tangent of the orbit. It does not point at the centre.
Paths pile up and get confusing. Use Clear often.
If a body leaves the screen, zoom out or press Return Objects.

my-solar-system.summary: Build your own solar system by laying the bodies out yourself. Mass, position and velocity can all be typed in as numbers, and you can put down several bodies at once.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. The basics, with two bodies.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: Put down several bodies and experiment freely. The three-body problem lives here.

controls.name: The bodies (drag them on screen)
controls.desc: Drag a body to move it, and drag the V arrow attached to it to set its velocity.
controls.tip: Placing them roughly by hand is fine. When you need exact values, type them in under More Data below.

controls.name: More Data (bottom left)
controls.desc: Open it and you can type in each body's Mass, Position (AU) and Speed (km/s) as numbers.
controls.tip: To rebuild the same conditions and compare, type the numbers in here. Dragging by hand comes out a little different every time.

controls.name: Bodies (bottom centre)
controls.desc: Sets how many bodies you are working with. On the Lab screen you can take it up to several.
controls.tip: Raise it to 3 and press play. The orbits do not settle easily - that is the famous three-body problem.

controls.name: Center of Mass (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Marks the shared centre that the two bodies really go round.
controls.tip: The key readout of this lesson. Check that it sits far closer to the heavy one, and that the two bodies go round that point together.

controls.name: Follow Center of Mass (bottom left)
controls.desc: Locks the view onto the centre of mass.
controls.tip: With it on, the star's wobble is far clearer. The star traces a small circle on the spot.

controls.name: Gravity Force · Velocity · Path · Grid · Measuring Tape (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Turn on the force arrows, the velocity arrows, the trail, the grid and a ruler.
controls.tip: Turn on Gravity Force and you can compare the lengths of the two bodies' force arrows. That is how you settle ② in this lesson.

controls.name: Zoom (right)
controls.desc: Changes the view scale, over a very wide range.
controls.tip: Zoom out when a body flies off. Zoom in to see the star's tiny wobble.

controls.name: Return Bodies and the clear-path button
controls.desc: Put the bodies back where they started, or wipe the paths.
controls.tip: If a body is slingshotted away and lost, press Return Bodies first.

steps: On the Intro screen turn on Gravity Force · Path · Grid.
Compare the lengths of the two gravity force arrows.
Press play and see whether the star moves too.
Reduce the star's Mass and watch the wobble grow.
Turn on Center of Mass and Follow Center of Mass.
Make the two masses nearly equal.
On the Lab screen take Bodies to 3 and press play.
gotchas: The two bodies' gravity force arrows are the same length. If they look different, an arrow has been clipped for being too small.
With three or more bodies the orbits do not settle easily. Not a fault - that is how it is.
Dragging by hand gives slightly different values every time. To repeat the same conditions, type them in under More Data.

keplers-laws.summary: See why an orbit is an ellipse, and how the speed varies along it. The screen names are Kepler's three laws, so going through them in order is the lesson.

screens.name: First Law
screens.what: An orbit is an ellipse and the star is at a focus. Change how squashed it is by dragging the planet.

screens.name: Second Law
screens.what: It sweeps equal areas in equal times. Measure the areas of the wedges.

screens.name: Third Law
screens.what: The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbit size. Check it on the graph.

screens.name: All Laws
screens.what: All three together on one screen.

controls.name: Eccentricity (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Shows how squashed the current orbit is. It is not a handle that sets the value. Tick it and a scale from 0 to 1 appears on the left. 0 is a circle; larger is a longer, thinner ellipse.
controls.tip: The main thing you work with here. Keep the value high or the difference between near and far will not be visible.

controls.name: Changing the orbit shape (drag on screen)
controls.desc: Drag the planet, or drag the velocity arrow (v) attached to it, and the orbit shape changes. Mercury · Earth · Eris · Nereid · Halley written on the eccentricity scale are markers for comparison only; pressing them does nothing.
controls.tip: Earth is nearly a circle and Halley is very long and thin. Comparing the two tells you what eccentricity is straight away.

controls.name: Axes · Foci · String · Semiaxes (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Draw the skeleton of the ellipse. Turn on Foci and you can see the star is at a focus, not at the centre.
controls.tip: Try String. Add the distances from the two foci to the planet and it is always the same - that is the definition of an ellipse.

controls.name: Velocity · Speed (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Show the velocity arrow and the speed as a number.
controls.tip: The tool for settling ② in this lesson. Write the numbers down close in and far out, and compare.

controls.name: Period Divisions (left of the Second Law screen)
controls.desc: Sets how many pieces one circuit is cut into. That many wedges get filled in.
controls.tip: About 6 looks best. Cut too finely and the areas are hard to compare.

controls.name: Area Values · Time Values (left of the Second Law screen)
controls.desc: Show each wedge's area and the time it took, as numbers.
controls.tip: Turn on Area Values. The shapes are all different and the areas are all the same - that is the whole law.

controls.name: The Period vs Semi-major Axis graph (Third Law screen)
controls.desc: Graphs the relationship between period and orbit size. The axes can be switched between T · T² · T³ and a · a² · a³.
controls.tip: Set them to T² and a³ and the points fall on a straight line. Other combinations curve - do try them.

controls.name: Target Orbit (top right) - Mercury · Venus · Earth · Mars · Jupiter
controls.desc: Draws a real planet's orbit over the top. Choosing one does not move your orbit there - it is for matching against.
controls.tip: Use it to compare the orbit you built against a real one. The difference in size is obvious at a glance.

controls.name: Always Circular (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Forces the orbit to stay a circle.
controls.tip: Good for flipping back and forth between ellipse and circle to compare the speed. On a circle the speed is constant.

controls.name: Star Mass · Zoom · Measuring Tape · Stopwatch
controls.desc: Change the mass of the central star, and use the scale and the measuring tools.
controls.tip: Raise the Star Mass and the period shortens for the same orbit. Worth looking at alongside the third law.

steps: On the First Law screen tick Eccentricity, then drag the planet to bring the orbit close to 0 and then out to a long thin ellipse.
Match your orbit against the Earth and Halley markers on the eccentricity scale and compare.
Turn on Velocity and Speed and note the speed close in and far out.
Turn on Foci and confirm the star sits at a focus.
On the Second Law screen set Period Divisions to 6 and press play.
Turn on Area Values and compare the wedge areas.
On the Third Law screen set the axes to T² and a³.
gotchas: The star sits at a focus of the ellipse, not at its centre. That is what creates a near side and a far side.
With a small eccentricity the difference in speed is barely visible. Keep it high while you experiment.
This sim was built for high school. The first and second laws alone are enough for this lesson.

states-of-matter.summary: Heat and cool matter magnified down to the grains. You can watch with your own eyes how solid, liquid and gas divide by the motion of the grains.

screens.name: States
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Heat and cool to move between the three states.

screens.name: Phase Changes
screens.what: You can apply Pressure as well as temperature, and turn a gas into a liquid with pressure alone.

screens.name: Interaction
screens.what: The force between two grains on its own. The push-when-close, pull-when-far relationship is drawn as a graph.

controls.name: Atoms & Molecules (top right) - Neon · Argon · Oxygen · Water
controls.desc: Choose the substance. The look of the grains and the force holding them both change.
controls.tip: Start with Neon. One round grain shows the motion most clearly. Leave Water until last - it has the odd property of arranging loosely as it freezes.

controls.name: Solid · Liquid · Gas (buttons on the right)
controls.desc: Press one and it switches straight to that state.
controls.tip: Press the three in turn to compare the arrangements, then use Heat / Cool to change slowly and watch the in-between.

controls.name: Heat · Cool (handle at the bottom)
controls.desc: Warms or chills it. The Temperature at the top left follows.
controls.tip: The main action here. Push it gently. Shove it and the state jumps, and you miss the change happening.

controls.name: The temperature readout (top left)
controls.desc: Shown in both K and ℃.
controls.tip: The ℃ side gives you a feel for it. Neon boils around −249 ℃ - it is only a liquid at very low temperatures.

controls.name: Pressure (Phase Changes screen)
controls.desc: Applies pressure to the container to squeeze the grains together.
controls.tip: Turn a gas into a liquid with pressure alone, without lowering the temperature. It is why the inside of a butane canister is liquid.

controls.name: Distance Between Atoms (Interaction screen)
controls.desc: Sets the distance between two grains directly. The Potential Energy curve below moves with it.
controls.tip: Close is Repulsive, far is Attractive. The curve is lowest at just the right distance, and that is the stable spot.

controls.name: Forces (right of the Interaction screen)
controls.desc: Choose between Hide Forces · Total Force · Attractive (van der Waals) and Repulsive (electron overlap).
controls.tip: Turn Attractive and Repulsive on separately and you can see why the total force has the shape it does. It is a contest between the two.

controls.name: The pause, step and slow-speed controls
controls.desc: Stop, advance a frame, or play slowly. The pause and step buttons are icons with no words on them.
controls.tip: To catch the moment a solid turns into a liquid, run it slowly.

steps: On the States screen choose Neon and press the Solid button.
Watch the grains shiver in their rows.
Push gently toward Heat, watching the temperature and the grains together.
Catch the moment it turns to liquid and then to gas.
Push toward Cool and take it back.
Change to Water and look at the arrangement as it freezes.
On the Phase Changes screen, turn a gas into a liquid with Pressure alone.
On the Interaction screen, change the distance and watch attraction and repulsion.
gotchas: Grains do not get bigger when you heat them. They only get faster.
The temperature at which a substance becomes liquid differs enormously. Neon is around −249 ℃.
Water arranges its grains loosely as it freezes, which is why ice floats - the opposite of most substances.
Shove the heat/cool handle and the state jumps right past. Push it gently.

gas-properties.summary: Heat, squeeze and resize a container of gas to see where pressure comes from. There is a Collision Counter, so you can count the grains drumming on the wall yourself.

screens.name: Ideal
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Temperature, volume, pressure and the number of grains, all free to change.

screens.name: Explore
screens.what: Measure the relationships under set conditions.

screens.name: Energy
screens.what: Shows the speed distribution of the grains. This is where you see they are not all at one speed.

screens.name: Diffusion
screens.what: Open the divider and watch two gases mix by themselves.

controls.name: The pump (bottom left)
controls.desc: Press it to put gas into the container. Under Particles above you can choose Heavy or Light ones.
controls.tip: Put in the same number of each and compare their speeds. Same temperature, and the heavy ones are slower.

controls.name: Hold Constant (right) - Nothing · Volume (V) · Temperature (T) · Pressure
controls.desc: Sets what stays fixed while you experiment.
controls.tip: The key switch in this sim. Fix one and the relationship between the other two shows itself. Fix nothing and several things move at once and you reach no conclusion.

controls.name: Heat · Cool (handle at the bottom)
controls.desc: Warms or chills the container.
controls.tip: Hold Volume (V) and then heat. The pressure rises cleanly on its own.

controls.name: The right-hand wall of the container (drag it)
controls.desc: Push or pull the wall to change the volume.
controls.tip: Hold Temperature (T) and push the wall. Only the relationship between volume and pressure is left.

controls.name: The pressure gauge (above the container)
controls.desc: Shown in both atm and kPa.
controls.tip: Where the answer appears in this sim. Write the value down before you change conditions.

controls.name: Collision Counter (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Counts Wall Collisions over a set time. The Sample Period can be changed too.
controls.tip: The best tool in this lesson. Watching the collision count rise alongside the pressure makes "pressure = drumming" concrete.

controls.name: Width · Stopwatch (checkboxes on the right)
controls.desc: Bring out a ruler for the container width and a stopwatch.
controls.tip: Turn on Width when you want to halve the volume exactly.

controls.name: Return Lid (above the container)
controls.desc: Puts the lid back after the pressure has blown it off.
controls.tip: Heat it enough and the lid flies off. Not a fault - the pressure passed the limit.

steps: Pump gas in and note the Pressure and Temperature.
Set Hold Constant to Volume (V).
Turn on the Collision Counter.
Heat it and watch the pressure and the collision count together.
Switch Hold Constant to Temperature (T) and push the wall in to reduce the volume.
Put heavy and light grains in together and compare their speeds.
Look at the speed distribution on the Energy screen.
Open the divider on the Diffusion screen.
gotchas: With Hold Constant on Nothing, several values move at once and you cannot see the relationship. Fix one and then experiment.
Heat it enough and the lid flies off. Put it back with Return Lid.
The grains' speeds are all different. Temperature is only an average.

molecule-shapes.summary: Attach bonds and lone pairs to a central atom and see how the shape of a molecule is settled. You can drag to rotate the view, so you can see the three-dimensional shape from several angles.

screens.name: Model
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Attach bonds and lone pairs as you like.

screens.name: Real Molecules
screens.what: Pick real molecules like H₂O · CO₂ · NH₃ · CH₄.

controls.name: Bonding (top right)
controls.desc: Attaches arms to the central atom. Single, double and triple bonds are available.
controls.tip: Single bonds alone are enough for this lesson. Change the number and watch how the shape changes.

controls.name: Lone Pair (right)
controls.desc: Attaches a pair of electrons that takes no part in bonding. No atom is attached, but it takes up room.
controls.tip: The heart of this sim. Make 2 bonds plus 2 lone pairs and you have the structure of water.

controls.name: Show Lone Pairs (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Shows or hides the lone pairs on screen.
controls.tip: Turn it off and on. With it off there is no telling why it bends - a device for showing you that something invisible is setting the shape.

controls.name: Show Bond Angles (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Shows the angle between bonds as a number.
controls.tip: Leave it on. By eye you cannot tell 104.5° from 109.5°.

controls.name: Molecule Geometry · Electron Geometry (bottom left, under Name)
controls.desc: Molecule Geometry is the shape of the atoms you can see; Electron Geometry is the shape counting the lone pairs as well.
controls.tip: The two can differ. Water is tetrahedral by electron geometry and bent by molecule geometry. That difference is the point of this lesson.

controls.name: Dragging to rotate the view
controls.desc: Drag an empty part of the screen and the molecule turns.
controls.tip: Do turn it. Seen from one direction only it looks flat and you will not recognise the tetrahedron.

controls.name: Remove All (right)
controls.desc: Takes off everything you have attached.
controls.tip: Press it before building a new structure. Clearing and starting again is quicker.

steps: On the Model screen turn on Molecule Geometry and Show Bond Angles.
Attach two bonds and watch it become linear.
Add Lone Pairs one at a time and watch it bend.
Read the angle at 2 bonds plus 2 lone pairs.
Turn Show Lone Pairs off and on.
Take the bonds to 3 and 4 and look at the shapes.
Drag to rotate the view and check it in three dimensions.
Compare H₂O against CO₂ on the Real Molecules screen.
gotchas: Lone pairs take up room too. Being invisible does not mean they have no effect on the shape.
Molecule Geometry (the shape you see) and Electron Geometry (counting the pairs) can differ.
The angle with 4 bonds is 109.5°, not 90°. Molecules are not flat.
Seen from one direction only you will read the shape wrongly. Drag to rotate.
This sim was built for high school. The Model screen alone is enough for this lesson.

molecule-polarity.summary: Shows which way a bond is lopsided as an arrow, and adds those arrows up to give the lopsidedness of the whole molecule. Adding vectors from course 02, used exactly as it stands.

screens.name: Two Atoms
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. The lopsidedness of one bond alone.

screens.name: Three Atoms
screens.what: Two bonds, and you can change the shape. The heart of this lesson is here.

screens.name: Real Molecules
screens.what: Pick real molecules like H₂O and CO₂.

controls.name: The Electronegativity handles (bottom) - Atom A · B · C
controls.desc: Set how hard each atom pulls on the electrons, from less to more.
controls.tip: Set two of them equal and the lopsidedness vanishes. Raise one alone and it tips that way - try both extremes first.

controls.name: Bond Dipole (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Draws the lopsidedness of each individual bond as a small arrow.
controls.tip: With no lopsidedness the arrow disappears. Present or absent is all you need to judge by.

controls.name: Molecular Dipole (checkbox on the right of the Three Atoms screen)
controls.desc: Draws the lopsidedness of the whole molecule as a big arrow. It is the bond arrows added together.
controls.tip: The key readout of this lesson. Leave it on together with the bond dipoles and change the shape. The moment the small arrows stay and only the big one goes is the answer.

controls.name: Dragging atoms to change the shape (Three Atoms screen)
controls.desc: Drag the outer atoms A and C to change the bond angle.
controls.tip: Go between straight and bent while watching the molecular dipole. That single action is the whole of this lesson.

controls.name: Partial Charges (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Marks δ+ and δ− - slightly positive and slightly negative.
controls.tip: This may be more intuitive than the arrows. The side the electrons have shifted to is δ−.

controls.name: Surface (Two Atoms screen) - None · Electrostatic Potential · Electron Density
controls.desc: Colours the outside of the molecule to show where the electrons have gathered.
controls.tip: Electrostatic Potential reads well. Red and blue put the lopsidedness in front of you at a glance.

controls.name: Electric Field (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Applies an electric field to the molecule.
controls.tip: A lopsided molecule turns to face the field; a non-polar one does not move. Another way of testing for polarity.

steps: On the Two Atoms screen turn on Bond Dipole and Partial Charges.
Set the two electronegativities equal and watch the arrow disappear.
Raise one alone and watch it reappear.
Move to the Three Atoms screen and turn on both Bond Dipoles and Molecular Dipole.
Straighten the molecule into a line and see what the big arrow does.
Bend it back again.
Turn on the Electric Field and see whether the molecule turns.
Compare H₂O against CO₂ on the Real Molecules screen.
gotchas: Even with lopsided bonds, a molecule can be un-lopsided. A symmetric shape cancels them.
Bond Dipole (the small arrows) and Molecular Dipole (the big one) are different things. You need both on to see the relationship.
Molecular Dipole only exists on the Three Atoms screen. With two atoms there is one bond, so the two are the same.
This sim was built for high school. Keep to the order Two Atoms → Three Atoms and you can follow it.

ph-scale.summary: Pour familiar liquids into a beaker and measure the pH. Add water or drain it away and watch the pH move. The scale on the left shows acidic, neutral and basic in colour.

screens.name: Macro
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Pour a real liquid and measure it with the pH meter.

screens.name: Micro
screens.what: Shows the H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ particles in the same liquid. Confirm grain by grain why the pH is what it is.

screens.name: My Solution
screens.what: Set the pH yourself and see what the particles do at that value.

controls.name: The liquid chooser (the dropper above the beaker)
controls.desc: Choose from familiar liquids - Battery Acid, Blood, Coffee, Milk, Orange Juice, Spit, Hand Soap, Drain Cleaner and more. Press the dropper to pour into the beaker.
controls.tip: Compare one acid against one base first. Measuring your way through the list gives you a feel for the scale quickly.

controls.name: The pH meter (left)
controls.desc: Drag it into the liquid and a pH value appears. Out of the liquid there is no reading.
controls.tip: The tip of the probe has to be inside the liquid. A reading of — means you have not dipped it yet.

controls.name: The water tap (top right)
controls.desc: Pours more water into the beaker, diluting the liquid.
controls.tip: The key action of this lesson. Pour water and watch the pH approach 7 without passing it.

controls.name: The drain (below the beaker)
controls.desc: Empties the liquid out. Use it to start again.
controls.tip: Empty it before changing liquids. Mixed together, there is no telling what made the pH what it is.

controls.name: The Acidic · Neutral · Basic scale (left)
controls.desc: A 0-14 scale in colour, with the current value marked on it.
controls.tip: On this scale one step is ten times. Read it like an ordinary ruler and you will badly misjudge the difference.

controls.name: The volume readout (½ L · 1 L)
controls.desc: Shows how much liquid is in the beaker.
controls.tip: Bring the volume up ten-fold with water and the pH moves by 1. Watching the volume as you pour makes the rule visible.

steps: Choose Orange Juice and pour it into the beaker.
Dip the pH meter and note the value.
Pour water in and watch which way the pH goes.
Fill the beaker and check whether it passes 7.
Empty it with the drain and do the same with Drain Cleaner.
Compare the particle counts on the Micro screen.
gotchas: On the pH scale one step is ten times. pH 4 and pH 6 are 100 times apart.
No amount of water turns an acid into a base. It only approaches 7.
The tip of the meter has to be under the liquid for a reading.
Empty it with the drain before changing liquids. Mixed, the result is unreadable.
This sim has three screens. The lesson opens only the Macro screen.

acid-base-solutions.summary: Put strong acid, weak acid, strong base and weak base side by side and compare them grain by grain. The power of this sim is that it shows not just the pH but what is in the beaker and how much of it.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Choose between five ready-made solutions and compare them.

screens.name: My Solution
screens.what: Set the concentration and the strength separately. The best screen for pulling the two ideas apart.

controls.name: The solution chooser (top right)
controls.desc: Choose between Water · Strong Acid · Weak Acid · Strong Base · Weak Base. The formula is in the brackets.
controls.tip: Flip between Strong Acid and Weak Acid and compare the beakers. That single contrast is the whole lesson.

controls.name: Views - Particles · Graph · Hide Views (bottom right)
controls.desc: Choose whether to look inside the beaker as grains, as a bar graph, or not at all.
controls.tip: Look at Particles first and confirm with Graph. The grains give you the feel; the graph gives you the exact amount.

controls.name: The equilibrium concentration graph (left)
controls.desc: Bars for H₃O⁺, OH⁻ and the unsplit molecules. The vertical axis is a log scale in powers of ten.
controls.tip: One step of a bar is ten times. A small-looking difference is really a large one. negligible at the bottom means "too little to matter".

controls.name: pH Color Key (top left)
controls.desc: Drag it into the liquid and it changes colour. Read the pH roughly from the colour.
controls.tip: The same as litmus paper in a real lab. Learning it by colour before numbers builds the instinct.

controls.name: The conductivity tester (left)
controls.desc: Dip both electrodes into the liquid and the bulb lights. The more ions, the brighter.
controls.tip: The most entertaining tool here. It turns an invisible degree of ionisation into brightness. Do compare the strong and weak acids.

controls.name: Initial Concentration · Strength (right of the My Solution screen)
controls.desc: Initial Concentration is how much you put in; Strength is how readily it splits. Two separate handles.
controls.tip: Move one at a time. How the beaker differs when you raise only the concentration against only the strength is the heart of this lesson.

steps: On the Intro screen set Views to Particles.
Choose Strong Acid and look inside the beaker.
Switch to Weak Acid and see the HA lumps left over.
Change to Graph and compare the height of the H₃O⁺ bars.
Dip the conductivity tester and compare the brightness.
On the My Solution screen, move concentration and strength one at a time.
gotchas: Strength (strong/weak) and concentration (concentrated/dilute) are different words. This sim exists to pull them apart.
The vertical axis of the graph is logarithmic. One step is ten times.
If the bulb does not light, check that both electrodes are under the liquid.
A short-circuit warning on the tester means there are a great many ions. Not a fault.

balancing-chemical-equations.summary: Put numbers in the boxes in front of each substance to make the atom counts match on both sides. The small numbers inside a formula cannot be touched at all - which is the rule the sim exists to teach.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Three easy equations.

screens.name: Equations
screens.what: Much harder equations, selectable by type of reaction.

screens.name: Game
screens.what: A check game at the level of your choosing.

controls.name: The boxes (in front of each substance in the equation)
controls.desc: The number that goes here is the coefficient. Change it with the up and down arrows. The only place in this sim you can change.
controls.tip: Try to change the small number inside a formula and you cannot. It is blocked, not broken - and that is the point of this lesson.

controls.name: The equation chooser (bottom of the screen, three buttons)
controls.desc: On the Intro screen, choose between Make Ammonia · Separate Water · Combust Methane.
controls.tip: Start with Separate Water. Only two elements, so it is the simplest.

controls.name: View (top right)
controls.desc: Choose between the particles picture, the balance scales picture, the bar chart picture and None. The first three carry pictures only, with no words; only the last is a word.
controls.tip: The balance scales picture is the most intuitive - level on both sides means you have it. The particles picture shows you why.

controls.name: The balance in the middle and the = / ≠ marks
controls.desc: An = appears when the atom counts match on both sides, a ≠ when they do not. Each element is marked separately.
controls.tip: With several elements, fix them one at a time. Fixing one and breaking another is normal; go back and forth a few times and the answer appears.

controls.name: Balanced (top left)
controls.desc: Appears when the equation is completely right.
controls.tip: You are not finished until this shows. Getting one element right will not do it.

controls.name: The reaction type chooser (bottom of the Equations screen)
controls.desc: Choose between Synthesis · Decomposition · Combustion.
controls.tip: Each type of reaction has equations of a different shape. Work through all three and the pattern appears.

controls.name: Simplified / Not Simplified (top of the Equations screen)
controls.desc: Tells you whether the coefficients can be reduced further.
controls.tip: Even with the counts matching, something like 2 : 4 : 2 that divides through by 2 is not yet tidied up.

steps: On the Intro screen choose Separate Water.
Set View to the balance scales picture.
Change the numbers in the boxes until the scales are level.
Check that Balanced appears.
Change View to the particles picture and check again.
Switch to Combust Methane for an equation with three elements.
gotchas: The small numbers inside a formula cannot be changed. They are blocked because changing one gives you a different substance.
With several elements, fixing one breaks another. That is normal - go back and forth.
Matching counts are not the answer if they can still be reduced. Check the Simplified mark.
A coefficient of 1 is usually left out when writing, but here you have to put 1 in the box.

reactants-products-and-leftovers.summary: Put ingredients in and see how much gets made and how much is left. The good thing about this sim is that it explains with sandwiches before it goes anywhere near chemistry.

screens.name: Sandwiches
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Make sandwiches out of bread and cheese, and learn the rule with no chemical vocabulary at all.

screens.name: Molecules
screens.what: The same rule with real chemical reactions - Make Water, Make Ammonia, Combust Methane.

screens.name: Game
screens.what: A check game where you fill in the blanks.

controls.name: The reaction chooser (top right)
controls.desc: On the Sandwiches screen, Cheese · Meat and Cheese · Custom; on the Molecules screen, Make Water · Make Ammonia · Combust Methane.
controls.tip: Custom is where you set the rule yourself.

controls.name: Before "Reaction" (the big box, middle left)
controls.desc: Sets how many of each ingredient to put in. Change with the up and down arrows.
controls.tip: Raise one ingredient only. Some raise the result and some do not - that is the limiting reactant.

controls.name: After "Reaction" (the big box, middle right)
controls.desc: Shows what was made (Products) and what is left (Leftovers).
controls.tip: Do watch the Leftovers box. What is left tells you which ingredient ran short.

controls.name: The rule shown at the top
controls.desc: Shows how many of each ingredient this reaction uses, as an equation. For sandwiches it reads like 2 bread + 1 cheese.
controls.tip: That ratio is everything. Set it against the ratio of what you have and you can see which will run out first without doing any arithmetic.

controls.name: The No "Reaction" mark
controls.desc: Appears when there are not enough ingredients to make anything.
controls.tip: Not a fault. If one ingredient is at 0, the result is 0 however much of the rest there is.

steps: On the Sandwiches screen choose Cheese.
Check the rule at the top (2 bread + 1 cheese).
Set bread to 10 and cheese to 3.
Check the Products and the Leftovers.
Raise the cheese one at a time and watch how the result changes.
Do the same with Make Water on the Molecules screen.
gotchas: The most plentiful ingredient does not decide the result. The one that runs out first does.
If one ingredient is 0 the result is 0. That is why No "Reaction" appears.
The Sandwiches screen and the Molecules screen are the same rule. Get it firmly from the sandwiches before moving on.
The quotation marks in Before "Reaction" · After "Reaction" are there to mark that a sandwich is not really a chemical reaction.

beers-law-lab.summary: Measure concentration by depth of colour. Make a solution on the first screen, then shine light through it on the second to measure how much is eaten. The same arrangement as a real laboratory spectrophotometer.

screens.name: Concentration
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Add solute and pour water to make a solution.

screens.name: Beer's Law
screens.what: Shine light through the solution you made and measure the absorbance. Concentration, cell width and wavelength can all be changed.

controls.name: The solute chooser (right of the Concentration screen)
controls.desc: Choose between coloured substances such as Potassium permanganate, Potassium dichromate and Copper(II) sulfate.
controls.tip: Pick something strongly coloured. Potassium permanganate (purple) shows the change best.

controls.name: Solid (shaker) · Solution (dropper)
controls.desc: Shake in the solid or drip in a ready-made solution. Choose the method on the right.
controls.tip: Shaking the solid in raises the concentration faster. The dropper is easier for fine adjustment.

controls.name: The water tap and the drain
controls.desc: Pour more water in, or drain the liquid away.
controls.tip: Pour water and the colour fades and the concentration drops. The amount of solute is unchanged and the concentration still moves - worth seeing.

controls.name: The concentration probe (Concentration screen)
controls.desc: Drag it into the liquid and the concentration appears as a number.
controls.tip: The tip has to be inside the liquid. Watching the colour and the number together builds the instinct.

controls.name: The Saturated! mark
controls.desc: Appears when no more will dissolve, with undissolved grains piling up at the bottom.
controls.tip: Not a fault. It means the water has reached its limit, and adding more will not raise the concentration.

controls.name: Concentration handle (bottom of the Beer's Law screen)
controls.desc: Sets the concentration of the solution directly.
controls.tip: Double it and see how many times the absorbance grows. Exactly twice.

controls.name: The cell width handle (the cell of liquid in the middle)
controls.desc: Changes the length of the path the light travels.
controls.tip: The solution is untouched and the absorbance changes. The most surprising part of this lesson - do try it.

controls.name: Absorbance / Transmittance (the detector on the right)
controls.desc: Absorbance is how much light was eaten; Transmittance is how much got through.
controls.tip: The two move in opposite directions. The same fact seen from what was eaten or what is left.

controls.name: Wavelength - Preset · Variable (left)
controls.desc: Preset sets it automatically to the wavelength that substance eats best. Variable lets you choose.
controls.tip: Move the wavelength a long way on Variable. Same solution, wildly different absorbance - every substance has its own colour that it eats.

steps: On the Concentration screen, choose Potassium permanganate and add it.
Dip the concentration probe and look at the value.
Pour water and watch the colour and the concentration fall together.
Move to the Beer's Law screen and set the detector to Absorbance.
Double the Concentration and compare the absorbance.
Leave the concentration alone and double the width of the cell.
Change the Wavelength and watch the absorbance change.
gotchas: Absorbance is proportional to both the concentration and the cell width. To measure a concentration you have to fix the width.
Once Saturated! shows, adding more will not raise the concentration.
A colourless solute barely eats any light, so the absorbance hardly registers. Pick something strongly coloured.

fractions-intro.summary: Turns a fraction into a picture. There is almost no text - changing two numbers changes the picture, and that is all of it, so five minutes is enough to get comfortable.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Change the numerator and denominator and the picture follows at once.

screens.name: Game
screens.what: Name the fraction from the picture. 10 levels. Good on your own once the lesson is done.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: A free space with no targets, where you drag pieces around as you like.

controls.name: The shape chooser (the box at the top centre)
controls.desc: Choose one of six: circle · horizontal bar · vertical bar · beaker · cake · number line. It sits just above the picture. Only the picture changes; the value of the fraction does not.
controls.tip: Seeing the same fraction in all six is the heart of this sim. The number line especially is the only one that shows a fraction is not a "piece" but a single number.

controls.name: Max (top right)
controls.desc: Sets how many containers you can use, from 1 to 6, with the round arrows.
controls.tip: Left at 1, you cannot make a fraction bigger than 1. If raising the numerator stops having any effect, check here.

controls.name: Numerator · Denominator (the large fraction, middle right)
controls.desc: The number above the line is the numerator and the one below is the denominator. Round arrows beside each raise and lower them. The denominator runs 1-8.
controls.tip: Change one and leave the other alone. Move both and you cannot tell what made the picture change.

controls.name: The piece tray (bottom centre)
controls.desc: You can also drag pieces into and out of the containers by hand. The numerator follows.
controls.tip: Raising the arrows and dragging pieces in give the same result. Use whichever suits.

steps: Choose the circle in the shape chooser.
Set the denominator to 3 and the numerator to 1 for 1/3.
Leave the numerator and raise the denominator alone to 8, watching how thin the piece gets.
Raise Max to 3 for three containers.
With denominator 4, raise the numerator to 12 and check the three containers fill exactly.
Change the shape chooser to the number line and see where the same fraction sits.
gotchas: Raise the denominator and the pieces get smaller. A bigger number feels like a bigger value; it is the opposite.
If raising the numerator does not fill the picture, Max is set to 1. You are short of containers, not broken.
Change the denominator and pieces already placed get re-cut. Nothing to be alarmed at - it is the same amount cut differently.
This sim has three screens. The lesson opens only the Intro screen.

fractions-equality.summary: Builds a fraction of equal value on the right automatically and shows it beside yours. A sim for checking, by area, whether the = in the middle is really telling the truth.

screens.name: Equality Lab
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Really a bench for comparing equal values side by side.

screens.name: Game
screens.what: Find fractions of equal value. 10 levels.

controls.name: The shape chooser (above and left of the = sign)
controls.desc: Four this time: circle · horizontal bar · vertical bar · beaker. Unlike the previous sim, cake and number line are not in this chooser.
controls.tip: Since you are comparing areas, the horizontal bar reads best. Circles get hard to judge by eye once the pieces are cut fine.

controls.name: Numerator · Denominator (the large fraction, bottom left)
controls.desc: Sets the left-hand fraction. The denominator runs 1-6 and there are at most 4 containers.
controls.tip: The right-hand fraction cannot be set directly. It is settled entirely by the left-hand one and the multiplier.

controls.name: The green arrow (bottom right end)
controls.desc: The multiplier, 1, 2 or 3, sitting immediately to the right of the multiplied fraction. The right-hand fraction is the left one with its numerator and denominator multiplied by it.
controls.tip: The most important control here. That raising it does not change the shaded area is the whole of this lesson.

controls.name: The picture / number line chooser (top right)
controls.desc: Chooses whether to see the right half only as a picture or as a number line. The left stays a picture.
controls.tip: The number line stands vertically. Raise the multiplier and the ticks get finer while the marked point stays at the same height. Area gets you as far as "they look similar"; this nails it as "the same number".

steps: Set the left-hand fraction to 3/4.
Raise the green arrow to 2 and watch the right become 6/8. Compare the areas.
Take the green arrow to 3 and check the area is still the same at 9/12.
Change the left to 5/6 and fix the shaded area in your mind.
Return to 3/4 and compare which is fuller.
Change the right-hand chooser to the number line and check the point stays at the same height as you raise the green arrow.
gotchas: The right-hand fraction is not yours to set. It follows automatically from the left-hand fraction times the green arrow.
The green arrow only goes up to 3. Larger multiples are not available here.
The denominator only goes up to 6. A fraction like 7/8 cannot be built here - use the previous sim (Fractions: Intro) for that.

fractions-mixed-numbers.summary: The controls are identical to Fractions: Intro. Exactly two things are added - the Mixed Number checkbox and the Equation box. Those two are the whole sim.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Where you turn improper fractions into mixed numbers.

screens.name: Game
screens.what: Name the mixed number. 10 levels.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: A free space with no targets, where you handle the pieces as you like.

controls.name: The shape chooser (top centre)
controls.desc: Six: circle, horizontal bar, vertical bar, beaker, cake and number line.
controls.tip: The number line is especially good for improper fractions. That 8/3 lies between 2 and 3 shows up immediately as a picture.

controls.name: Max (top right)
controls.desc: Sets how many containers you can use - here 1-4.
controls.tip: The previous sim went to 6 and this one to 4. With a large whole part the picture gets messy, so it was cut back.

controls.name: Numerator · Denominator (the large fraction, middle right)
controls.desc: The denominator runs 1-8. Being able to raise the numerator above the denominator is the point of this sim.
controls.tip: Set the numerator to a multiple of the denominator (3, 6, 9…) and the display becomes a whole number. That is where you see the division come out even.

controls.name: Mixed Number (bottom right, above the reset button)
controls.desc: On, the large display changes into a mixed number like 2 and 2/3. Off, it stays 8/3.
controls.tip: Turn it on and off repeatedly. Once you see it is two name tags on one picture, improper fractions and mixed numbers stop being confusing.

controls.name: Equation (collapsible box, bottom left)
controls.desc: Press the title to open it. It writes out how the fraction was split.
controls.tip: If the Mixed Number checkbox shows you the "result", this box shows you the "working". Open it when you cannot see why the answer came out that way.

steps: Set the denominator to 3 and the numerator to 8 for 8/3.
Count the full containers and the pieces left over.
Tick Mixed Number and watch the display become 2 and 2/3.
Open the Equation box and check how it was split.
Raise the numerator to 9 and watch the display become the whole number 3.
Change the shape to the number line and confirm 8/3 lies between 2 and 3.
gotchas: The Mixed Number checkbox changes only the display. The value is unchanged - 8/3 and 2 and 2/3 are the same number.
If raising the numerator does not fill the picture, Max is too low. It only goes to 4 here.
When it comes out to a whole number the fraction part of the mixed number disappears. It is not lost - it is 0/3, so it is not written.
The screen is nearly identical to Fractions: Intro, which is confusing. If you can see the Mixed Number checkbox, you are in this one.

build-a-fraction.summary: The opposite of everything so far. The screen does not draw for you - you drag pieces in to make the target fraction. This sim starts at the level chooser - open it and you get level buttons before any game.

screens.name: Build a Fraction
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. Build fractions smaller than 1 out of pieces.

screens.name: Mixed Numbers
screens.what: The same game with fractions bigger than 1. Come here after lesson 3 (Fractions: Mixed Numbers).

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: A free space with no targets and no score. Use the pieces and number cards as you like.

controls.name: The level buttons (the first screen when you open it)
controls.desc: The buttons come in two rows. The top row builds with shapes and the bottom row with number cards. Only five show at a time; the yellow arrow at the bottom centre moves you across to levels 6-10.
controls.tip: Start with the top row. The bottom row has no pictures and has to be built in your head, which is much harder.

controls.name: The piece tray (bottom)
controls.desc: Pieces stacked by size from 1/1 down to 1/8. Drag them into the container on the left.
controls.tip: Fill the same target with different pieces too. That is exactly what this sim is here to teach.

controls.name: Green + · red − (right of the container)
controls.desc: Adds or removes a container. Used for fractions bigger than 1.
controls.tip: With one container you cannot make a fraction bigger than 1. When the target passes 1, press the green + first.

controls.name: ◀ ▶ (under the container)
controls.desc: Changes how many pieces the container is cut into, from whole down to eighths. Set this first or a piece of that size will not go in.
controls.tip: If a piece will not go in, it is usually because the container is cut into a size that does not match. Check here first.

controls.name: The target boxes (right)
controls.desc: The fractions you have to make. Drag a finished group onto a box.
controls.tip: Right, and it settles in; wrong, and it simply comes back. Nothing is lost, so put it down even when you are not sure.

controls.name: The undo arrow (left of a group)
controls.desc: Takes the pieces out of that group one at a time. Only visible while the group is selected.
controls.tip: If you cannot see it, press the group once to select it. It only appears on the selected group.

controls.name: Back · refresh (top left)
controls.desc: Back returns to the level chooser. Refresh draws a new set of problems at the same level.
controls.tip: Refresh is useful when one problem has you stuck. It keeps the level and swaps the problems.

steps: On the Build a Fraction screen press Level 1 in the top row.
Pick a target fraction on the right and fill the container with pieces from the tray.
Once it is full, drag the group onto the target box.
Fill a 1/2 target using 1/6 pieces only.
Fill the same target again with different pieces.
Move up to levels 4-5 and meet a problem that needs the green +.
Use the house button to play the same game on the Mixed Numbers screen.
gotchas: Do not be thrown when no game appears as you open it. This one asks you to pick a level first.
It is easy to miss that the level buttons come in two rows. The top row (shapes) and the bottom row (number cards) are completely different games. Levels 6-10 are beyond the yellow arrow.
A piece that will not go into a container is not a fault - the division does not match. Set it with the ◀ ▶ under the container.
Getting it wrong costs you nothing. It just comes back. Try freely.
This sim has three screens. The lesson starts on Build a Fraction, but the others are open too.

fraction-matcher.summary: A game of pairing two cards of equal value on a balance. This sim also starts at the level chooser. The balance both marks your answer and tells you which side is bigger.

screens.name: Fractions
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. It starts below 1 and mixes in bigger fractions as the levels rise.

screens.name: Mixed Numbers
screens.what: The same game with mixed numbers. Cards like 1 and 1/4 turn up.

controls.name: The level buttons (the first screen when you open it)
controls.desc: There are 8 levels. 1 is the easiest and 8 the hardest.
controls.tip: Level 1 only has pictures and numbers that match exactly. From 2 on you have to reduce.

controls.name: The clock button (below the level chooser)
controls.desc: Turns the timer on and off. On, the elapsed time shows during the game.
controls.tip: Leave it off to begin with. Under time pressure you will guess instead of reducing. Turning it on later makes good practice.

controls.name: The cards
controls.desc: Picture cards and number cards laid out together. Drag them about.
controls.tip: Picture cards can pair with picture cards. Assume it is only picture ↔ number and you will flounder.

controls.name: The balance (middle)
controls.desc: Put one card on each pan. Right, and it goes level; wrong, and it tips toward the bigger side.
controls.tip: The most useful part of this sim. Getting it wrong tells you which side is bigger, so there is more to learn here than in getting it right.

controls.name: Check · Try Again · Show Answer
controls.desc: With both cards on, Check appears. Wrong, and you get Try Again; wrong a second time and Show Answer appears.
controls.tip: Show Answer places the right pair for you. It scores nothing, but you get to see why they are a pair.

controls.name: My Matches (the row at the top)
controls.desc: Pairs you have got right collect here. Fill all six and the level is over.
controls.tip: Press a collected pair again and you can put it back on the balance to check. Good for revision.

controls.name: Score · time (top)
controls.desc: Right first time is 2 points, right second time is 1. Six pairs, so full marks is 12.
controls.tip: Short of full marks means you guessed somewhere. The scoring is built so that getting it right first time pays.

steps: On the Fractions screen choose Level 1.
Drag two cards onto the pans and press Check.
Put a wrong pair on deliberately once and watch which way the balance tips.
Match all six pairs to finish a level.
Move to level 3 or above and watch fractions bigger than 1 come in.
Use the house button to play the same game on the Mixed Numbers screen.
gotchas: Do not be thrown when no game appears as you open it. This one asks you to pick a level first.
Pairs are not only picture ↔ number. Picture ↔ picture and number ↔ number count too, as long as the values match.
Do not shrug off a tipped balance. The direction it tips is information - it tells you which side is bigger.
From the second attempt a correct answer is worth 1 point. Reduce it in your head before you rush the cards up.
Leaving the timer on makes you hasty. Better off at first.

ratio-and-proportion.summary: Drag the two hands on screen up and down to hit a ratio. You do not have to look at any numbers - when the ratio is right the background deepens and the sound changes. Learn it by eye and ear first and turn the numbers on later.

screens.name: Discover
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Hit the set ratios (Challenge 1, 2, 3).

screens.name: Create
screens.what: Set a ratio yourself and hit it. You can also lock the two hands to move together.

controls.name: The two hands (middle of the screen)
controls.desc: Drag each up and down. The ratio of the two heights is the current ratio.
controls.tip: The one key action here. Break the ratio by moving one hand alone, then raise both together and confirm the ratio holds.

controls.name: The background colour and the sound
controls.desc: The closer the ratio, the deeper the background and the steadier the sound. Off the ratio, it fades.
controls.tip: This is the real marker in this sim. Hit the ratio by colour and sound before you look at numbers - it is built to teach ratio as a feel.

controls.name: Challenge 1 · 2 · 3 (right of the Discover screen)
controls.desc: Choose the ratio to hit. It does not tell you what the ratio is.
controls.tip: Hit it by colour and sound without knowing the numbers, then turn the tick marks on to see what it was. That order is the design intent.

controls.name: The tick mark chooser (top right, three buttons)
controls.desc: Three buttons with pictures only and no words. From the left: no tick marks (a crossed-out eye), tick marks (horizontal lines) and numbered tick marks (lines with numbers).
controls.tip: Start on no tick marks. With numbers visible you will solve it by arithmetic instead of by feel.

controls.name: Range (right of the Create screen)
controls.desc: Choose how far the hands can move - 0 to 10 · 0 to 20 · 0 to 30.
controls.tip: The same ratio can be hit with bigger numbers on a wider range. Good for confirming that 2 : 3 and 20 : 30 are the same.

controls.name: My Challenge (right of the Create screen)
controls.desc: Set the left and right values yourself to make your own problem.
controls.tip: Make one to set a friend. Becoming the person who sets the ratio deepens the understanding a lot.

controls.name: Ratio Lock (bottom right of the Create screen)
controls.desc: On, the two hands move together, keeping the ratio.
controls.tip: Do turn it on. You can feel with your hand that the ratio holds while only the size changes. That is what "a ratio is a relationship, not a size" means.

steps: On the Discover screen choose Challenge 1.
With the tick marks off, hit the ratio by colour and sound alone.
Once you have it, press the third tick mark button (numbered) to see what it was.
Set the left hand to 2 and the right to 3, then raise the left alone to 4.
Find what the right hand has to be to match again.
On the Create screen turn on Ratio Lock and raise both hands together.
gotchas: The tick mark buttons have no words on them. Tell them apart by picture: from the left, no tick marks, tick marks, numbered tick marks.
A ratio is not kept by adding. Adding 2 to one side does not mean adding 2 to the other - you have to multiply both by the same factor.
If you cannot hear anything, check your device volume or the sound button at the top right of the sim. Half of this sim is sound.

proportion-playground.summary: Shows how the same ratio works in four completely different places. The picture buttons at the bottom centre switch between them - there are no words, so you choose by picture.

screens.name: Explore
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Change the values and the result shows at once.

screens.name: Predict
screens.what: The result is hidden so you can guess before opening it. Come here after Explore.

controls.name: The place chooser (bottom centre, four picture buttons)
controls.desc: Choose between necklace · billiard table · paint · apples. Pictures only, no words.
controls.tip: Do all four. That one rule turns up as colour, as pattern, as angle and as price - that is the whole sim.

controls.name: The two value handles
controls.desc: Each place has two values - bead counts, length and width, paint amounts, apple count and price.
controls.tip: Change one alone and watch the result change, then multiply both by the same factor and watch it stay. Those two contrasts are the point.

controls.name: The paint place
controls.desc: Set the amounts of the two colours and the mixed colour appears below.
controls.tip: Compare 1 : 2 against 3 : 6. Same colour. Then change to 2 : 6 and it shifts sharply.

controls.name: The billiard table place - Length · Width
controls.desc: Set the table's length and width and the path the ball bounces along is drawn.
controls.tip: Try doubling both. The table grows and the shape of the path does not. That is what "similar" looks like.

controls.name: The necklace place
controls.desc: The ratio of the two kinds of bead sets the repeating pattern.
controls.tip: Add beads to lengthen the necklace and the pattern is unchanged. Another example of a ratio setting a shape.

controls.name: The apples place - Total Cost · Cost per Apple
controls.desc: Set the number of apples and the total cost and it gives you the cost per apple.
controls.tip: A trailer for the next lesson (unit rates). Get used to what one costs here and lesson 3 is much easier.

controls.name: The cover button (Predict screen)
controls.desc: Hides the result, then reveals it.
controls.tip: Say your answer first and then open it. Opening it straight away is no practice at all.

steps: On the Explore screen choose the paint place.
Set 1 : 2 and fix the colour in your mind.
Change to 3 : 6 and see whether the colour is the same.
Change to 2 : 6 and watch it change this time.
On the billiard table place, double both the length and the width.
On the apples place, see how the cost per apple comes out.
gotchas: The place chooser has no words on it. Change places with the picture buttons at the bottom centre.
Increasing the amount and changing the ratio are different things. Double the paint and you get more of it, not a deeper colour.
Lengthen one side alone of the billiard table and the path changes. To stay similar, both need the same factor.
Go to the Predict screen only after plenty of Explore. In the other order it is just guessing.

unit-rates.summary: Convert prices into what one costs and compare. The Double Number Line at the top is the centre of this sim, so the practice is reading off the line instead of calculating.

screens.name: Shopping
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Buy and sell fruit, vegetables and sweets and work with unit rates.

screens.name: Shopping Lab
screens.what: Set the prices and counts yourself to make your own problems.

screens.name: Racing Lab
screens.what: Time and distance instead of money. The unit rate becomes speed.

controls.name: The item chooser (left)
controls.desc: Apples, Lemons, Oranges, Pears, Carrots, Cucumbers, Potatoes, Tomatoes, candy and more. Prices differ by kind.
controls.tip: Note the unit rate of two items and compare them. The best way to use this sim.

controls.name: The Double Number Line (top centre)
controls.desc: Two number lines drawn side by side. The top is dollars and the bottom is the count.
controls.tip: The key tool here. The two lines growing in step is what the same ratio means, which is why knowing one side lets you read the other off without calculating.

controls.name: Unit Rate? (in the Questions box)
controls.desc: Tells you what one costs.
controls.tip: The number this sim exists to teach. Whatever else you skip, check this one.

controls.name: Questions (collapsible box on the right)
controls.desc: Problems like "Cost of 10 Apples?". Type an answer and it tells you whether it is right.
controls.tip: Answer in your head first, then read it off the double number line to check. The two methods have to agree.

controls.name: The scale and the price tag (middle)
controls.desc: Put items on the scale or change the count and the price follows.
controls.tip: Some items are sold by weight (pounds). Only the basis changes from count to weight; the rule is the same.

controls.name: Erase (right)
controls.desc: Clears the marks you have made on the double number line.
controls.tip: Press it when the marks pile up and get confusing. The item and the prices stay.

steps: On the Shopping screen choose an item.
Check the Unit Rate? and note it down.
Raise the count 1 → 2 → 3 and watch the two lines grow in step.
Open the Questions box, answer first, then check on the double number line.
Change items and compare the unit rates.
Do the same with time and distance on the Racing Lab.
gotchas: A cheaper total is not the better buy. You have to look at the cost of one to compare.
Items sold in pounds go by weight, not count. That is why decimals turn up.
The purpose of this sim is reading off the double number line rather than getting the questions right.

mean-share-and-balance.summary: Builds a mean as a picture rather than a formula. Connect cups with pipes and let the water level out, share apples among people, or find the balance point of a see-saw. All three are the same mean in the end.

screens.name: Level Out
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Connect cups with pipes and make the water levels even.

screens.name: Distribute
screens.what: Share candy bars out among people and watch the mean per person.

screens.name: Fair Share
screens.what: Apples instead of water, shared among people. When they will not divide exactly, pieces appear.

screens.name: Balance Point
screens.what: Shows the mean as the fulcrum where a see-saw balances.

controls.name: Number of Cups · Number of People (bottom)
controls.desc: Sets how many cups or people you are working with, up to 7.
controls.tip: Start with 3. With many of them it is hard to follow what is happening.

controls.name: The cup handles (under each cup)
controls.desc: Sets the water level in each cup separately.
controls.tip: Fill them deliberately unevenly. Fill them evenly and opening the pipes does nothing at all.

controls.name: The pipes (between the cups)
controls.desc: Open them and water moves between cups until every level is the same.
controls.tip: The key action of this sim. Predict the result before you open them. That prediction is the mean calculation.

controls.name: Predict Mean · Tick Marks (right)
controls.desc: Mark the level you think it will be before you see the answer.
controls.tip: Mark first, then open the pipes, and how far off you were is right there. The best practice in this sim.

controls.name: Sync · Collect · Share (middle of the Fair Share screen)
controls.desc: Buttons to gather the apples up (Collect) and share them out evenly (Share).
controls.tip: Press Collect then Share. Those two actions - gathering everything and dividing it equally - are the two halves of the mean formula.

controls.name: Total (top right)
controls.desc: Shows the total amount of whatever you are working with.
controls.tip: Check that the total does not change across opening the pipes. Taking a mean leaves the whole untouched.

controls.name: Mean (collapsible box, top left)
controls.desc: Shows the mean and how it was worked out.
controls.tip: Open it after you have understood the picture. Open it first and you will look at the formula and move on.

controls.name: The info button (middle)
controls.desc: Tells you what the current screen is about.
controls.tip: Each screen handles something different, so press it when you lose track.

steps: On the Level Out screen set Number of Cups to 3.
Fill the water levels unevenly at 2 · 4 · 6.
Mark your answer first with Predict Mean.
Open the pipes and compare against the real level.
Take the cups up to 7 and do the same.
On the Fair Share screen press Collect then Share.
On the Balance Point screen watch the mean appear as the fulcrum.
gotchas: Fill the cups evenly and opening the pipes changes nothing. Fill them unevenly on purpose.
The water neither grows nor shrinks. What was there was simply spread out evenly - that is what a mean means.
When the apples will not divide exactly, pieces appear. Not an error - the result of a division can be a fraction.
There are four screens and they get harder. Level Out → Fair Share → Balance Point is the order to take.

graphing-lines.summary: The graph on the left, the equation on the right. They are joined, so dragging a point on the graph changes the equation and changing a number in the equation moves the line. Work from either side.

screens.name: Slope
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. See how two points settle a slope.

screens.name: Slope-Intercept
screens.what: Works in the y = mx + b form. Lesson 2 uses it properly - you can skip it here.

screens.name: Point-Slope
screens.what: Fixes a line from one point and a slope. A brief visit at the end of lesson 1.

screens.name: Line Game
screens.what: A six-level check game. Draw the line from the equation, or make the equation from the line.

controls.name: The points on the graph (left)
controls.desc: Drag a round point and the line follows and the equation on the right changes at once.
controls.tip: The main action here. Land them exactly on the grid and the values come out whole, which makes the arithmetic easy.

controls.name: The numbers in the equation (top right)
controls.desc: Each number in the equation has up and down arrows. Press them and the graph follows.
controls.tip: Dragging the graph and changing the equation are the same thing. Use the equation when you need an exact value and the graph when you want the feel.

controls.name: The slope value (top right of the graph)
controls.desc: Shows the current slope as a fraction, written as the vertical difference over the horizontal difference.
controls.tip: Check here which of the two is the vertical one. It stops you memorising the slope upside down.

controls.name: Save Line · Erase Lines (right)
controls.desc: Save Line leaves the current line on screen in a faded colour. Erase Lines clears everything you have left.
controls.tip: The most useful button in this sim. Save before you change and you can see before and after side by side. Do not rely on memory.

controls.name: Line Game - choosing a level
controls.desc: Six levels. The higher you go, the less information you are given.
controls.tip: From level 3 it gives you two points and asks for the equation. Lesson 1 alone is enough to solve it.

steps: On the Slope screen, drag the two points about.
Set the points to (1, 2) and (3, 8) and read the slope.
Run the line down to the right and watch the slope go negative.
Make the line horizontal and then vertical and see what each gives.
Keep one with Save Line and compare it against a line of a different slope.
On the Point-Slope screen, see one point and a slope fix a line.
gotchas: Slope is the vertical difference over the horizontal. Flip it and your answer is the reciprocal.
A vertical line reads slope undefined. Not infinite - no value at all, because it would mean dividing by 0.
Saved lines stay faded on screen. When they get confusing, tidy up with Erase Lines.
This sim has four screens. The Slope-Intercept screen belongs to lesson 2.

graphing-slope-intercept.summary: The Slope-Intercept screen only, lifted out of the previous sim (Graphing Lines). The controls are identical so there is nothing new to learn, but the Line Game here is built around y = mx + b.

screens.name: Slope-Intercept
