screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. The equation is fixed in the form y = m x + b.

screens.name: Line Game
screens.what: A six-level game. The back half of this lesson happens here.

controls.name: m (slope) · b (y-intercept) - the equation at the top right
controls.desc: Change the two numbers in the equation with the up and down arrows. m can be set as a fraction.
controls.tip: Change one at a time, always. Move both and you cannot tell which did what. That distinction is the whole lesson.

controls.name: The handles on the graph (left)
controls.desc: There are two points on the line. Drag the one on the y axis and b changes; drag the other and m changes.
controls.tip: Dragging the point on the y axis is how you feel with your hand that b is the height at which it meets the y axis.

controls.name: Save Line · Erase Lines (right)
controls.desc: Leave the current line faded on screen, or clear what you have left.
controls.tip: Save the line with b changed alone and the one with m changed alone and put all three on one screen. The difference is obvious at a glance.

controls.name: Line Game - choosing a level
controls.desc: Six levels. Three kinds of problem: draw the line, make the equation, put points on the line.
controls.tip: It is fine to get them wrong. The game overlays the correct line, and the direction yours is off tells you at once whether you had m wrong or b wrong.

steps: Set the equation to y = 2x + 3.
Raise b alone to 5 and watch how the line moves.
Raise m alone to 4 and see what changes this time.
Keep one with Save Line and compare against a negative m.
Set b to 0 and watch the line pass through the origin.
Play Line Game levels 1 to 3.
gotchas: b does not change the slope. It only slides the whole line up and down.
Change m and the line turns about the y-intercept. That one point stays put.
The two points on the graph do different jobs. The one on the y axis is the b side.
The screen is nearly identical to the previous sim. If there are only two screens, you are in this one.

graphing-quadratics.summary: Drive a parabola from its equation. Each screen uses a different form of the equation - the same parabola written different ways - so checking which screen you are on matters.

screens.name: Explore
screens.what: y = a x² + b x + c, moved freely with sliders. Start here.

screens.name: Standard Form
screens.what: The same equation with whole-number values, showing Roots · Vertex · Axis of Symmetry together.

screens.name: Vertex Form
screens.what: y = a(x − h)² + k. The best screen for seeing where the vertex goes. The back half of this lesson happens here.

screens.name: Focus & Directrix
screens.what: The focus of a parabola. Beyond this lesson - visit later if you are curious.

controls.name: The a · b · c sliders (Explore, top right)
controls.desc: Move the three values of y = a x² + b x + c.
controls.tip: Start with a. It is a that sets the width and the direction. The effect of b is confusing, so leave it at 0 to begin with.

controls.name: The a · h · k sliders (Vertex Form, top right)
controls.desc: The three values of y = a(x − h)² + k. h handles left and right, k up and down.
controls.tip: A positive h moves the parabola right. It is written as a subtraction in the formula and moves right, which is the point of this screen.

controls.name: Quadratic Terms (Explore checkbox)
controls.desc: Draws the x² part on its own, overlaid on the whole parabola.
controls.tip: Worth having on while you look at how a sets the width. It separates out which part makes the curve.

controls.name: Vertex (checkbox)
controls.desc: Marks the vertex with a point and shows its coordinates.
controls.tip: Do turn it on. With it off there is nothing to check while you move h and k on the Vertex Form screen.

controls.name: Axis of Symmetry (checkbox)
controls.desc: Draws a vertical line through the vertex.
controls.tip: Shows that the parabola folds like a mirror about that line. The x value of the axis is the x value of the vertex.

controls.name: Roots (Standard Form checkbox)
controls.desc: Marks where the parabola meets the x axis. If it does not, it says NO REAL ROOTS.
controls.tip: Lift the parabola clear of the x axis. NO REAL ROOTS appears - a picture of what "no roots" means.

controls.name: Equations · Coordinates (checkboxes)
controls.desc: Put the equation beside the graph, or coordinates on each point.
controls.tip: Leave Coordinates on and you can read the vertex values off by eye and check them against your arithmetic.

steps: On the Explore screen, raise and lower a alone and watch the width.
Take a negative and watch the parabola flip.
Take a to 0 and confirm you get a straight line.
Move to the Vertex Form screen and turn on the Vertex checkbox.
Set h to 3 and see which way the vertex goes.
Move k and confirm this one goes with its sign.
gotchas: Raise a and the parabola gets narrower. The opposite of the "bigger means wider" feeling.
The vertex of y = (x − 3)² is at x = 3. A subtraction that moves it right. Find the x that makes the bracket 0 and it will not confuse you.
k goes with its sign. Only h is backwards.
Each screen uses a different form. a, b, c means Explore or Standard Form; a, h, k means Vertex Form.
This sim was built for high school. This lesson does not use the Focus & Directrix screen.

calculus-grapher.summary: The screen is in two panels. Draw a curve by hand in the top panel and the slope graph of that curve is drawn live in the bottom one.

screens.name: Derivative
screens.what: The screen this lesson uses. The bottom panel is the slope graph.

screens.name: Integral
screens.what: The other direction. The bottom panel draws the area under the curve. Not used in this lesson.

screens.name: Advanced
screens.what: Goes as far as the slope of the slope. Much harder.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: A screen for drawing freely with no target.

controls.name: The shape buttons (right, four icons)
controls.desc: Choose the shape to draw in the top panel - hill · pedestal · tilt · shift. Pictures only, with no words.
controls.tip: Choose tilt (the diagonal picture) to make a straight slope and hill (the peak picture) to make a hill. This lesson only uses those two.

controls.name: The curve in the top panel (drag it directly)
controls.desc: Drag in the top panel and the curve changes on the spot, according to the shape button you chose.
controls.tip: Drag slowly and watch the bottom panel. How the bottom follows while you work on the top is the whole sim. Look only when you have finished and you miss it.

controls.name: Tangent (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Puts a tangent line in the top panel. Drag it left and right and it measures the slope at that place.
controls.tip: Turn it on and drag from the uphill of a hill to the top and down the other side. Why the sign of the bottom graph changes becomes obvious.

controls.name: Slope of Tangent (the vertical gauge at the left edge)
controls.desc: Shows the slope where the tangent sits, as a bar. Up is +, down is −.
controls.tip: The height of this bar and the height of the bottom graph are always the same - one value shown two ways.

controls.name: Reference Line (checkbox on the right)
controls.desc: Puts a vertical line through both panels. You can drag it left and right.
controls.tip: The tool for comparing the top and bottom graphs at the same x. Turn it on when lining them up by eye is hard.

controls.name: The undo and reset buttons (right)
controls.desc: Undo the last thing you drew, or put the curve back to the start.
controls.tip: When the curve gets into a mess, reset first. Redrawing from scratch is faster than repairing it.

controls.name: Predict (top left / top right toggle)
controls.desc: Switches to a mode where you draw the bottom graph yourself and check it against the answer.
controls.tip: Good for testing yourself once the lesson is done - draw the bottom graph first and then open the answer.

controls.name: Show (top)
controls.desc: Shows or hides the original curve f(x).
controls.tip: Used in Predict mode to hide the answer for a moment.

steps: Choose the tilt shape and make a straight slope in the top panel.
Check the bottom panel is a horizontal line, and that its height rises as you make the slope steeper.
Tilt the slope the other way and check the line below goes below 0.
Choose the hill shape and draw a hill.
Turn on Tangent and drag it uphill → top → downhill.
Turn on the Reference Line and compare the two graphs at the same x.
gotchas: The top and bottom panels have different meanings on the vertical axis. The top is height and the bottom is slope. They must not be read as overlaid.
The shape buttons have no words on them. Tell them apart by picture.
This sim was built for high school and university. This lesson uses only the Derivative screen.

natural-selection.summary: Run a population of rabbits through many generations and watch how the proportions of a trait change. Mutation and environmental factors can be switched on separately, so you can confirm for yourself that it takes both to produce a change.

screens.name: Intro
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. The background is fixed and only the basic controls are there.

screens.name: Lab
screens.what: Set the environment and the conditions more freely. You can switch between snow and bare earth.

controls.name: Add a Mate · Play · Start Over (top centre)
controls.desc: Gives the single rabbit a mate and starts it breeding. After that the generations advance by themselves.
controls.tip: The experiment does not start until you press this. Before that, one rabbit sits there doing nothing.

controls.name: Add Mutation (top right)
controls.desc: Choose Fur · Ears · Teeth and put a new trait into the population. You can make it Dominant or Recessive.
controls.tip: Put it in as Dominant and the change shows quickly. A recessive one hides for a while before it appears, which is much slower.

controls.name: Environmental Factors (right) - Wolves · Tough Food · Limited Food
controls.desc: The selection pressure that decides what is favoured. Nothing has a direction until you switch one on.
controls.tip: The key switch of this lesson. Compare the proportions before and after switching one on and natural selection appears in one go. Different traits suit different factors - fur goes with wolves, teeth with food.

controls.name: The graph chooser (bottom right) - Population · Proportions · Pedigree · None
controls.desc: Population is head count, Proportions is the share held by each trait, and Pedigree shows the descendants of one rabbit.
controls.tip: Proportions suits this lesson best. Whether the head count rises or falls, how the shares change is what natural selection is.

controls.name: Turning trait lines on (the graph on the left)
controls.desc: Choose what to show from White Fur · Brown Fur · Straight Ears · Floppy Ears · Short Teeth · Long Teeth.
controls.tip: Leave only the two traits you are experimenting with switched on and the graph is far easier to read.

controls.name: Data Probe (the probe on the graph)
controls.desc: Drag it onto the graph and it reads the exact values for that generation.
controls.tip: Use it when you want to know "around which generation did it flip".

controls.name: Alleles (bottom left)
controls.desc: Shows the proportions of dominant and recessive genes as F/f · E/e · T/t.
controls.tip: The proportions of the appearance (fur colour) and of the genes can differ. A recessive gene stays in the population without showing.

controls.name: The pause button and the round reset button
controls.desc: Stop, or start again from the beginning. Both are icons with no words on them - the reset is the yellow circle at the bottom right.
controls.tip: Too many rabbits and the screen gets crowded. When you want to change conditions and go again, Reset All is quickest.

steps: Press Add a Mate to start the breeding.
Under Add Mutation, add Brown Fur as Dominant.
Set the graph to Proportions and turn on the white and brown fur lines.
Watch the proportions barely move while there is no environmental factor.
Turn on Wolves and watch the proportions change.
Watch to see whether any individual rabbit changes colour.
On the Lab screen, change the background to snow and watch the advantage flip.
gotchas: No individual rabbit changes colour. What changes is the proportions in the population.
Add a mutation alone without switching on an environmental factor and almost nothing happens. You need both.
Added as recessive it stays out of sight for a long while. Not a fault - that is how it works.
Too strong a selection pressure can wipe the whole population out. That happens in reality too.
Too many rabbits and it slows down. Switching on Limited Food keeps the numbers in check.

membrane-transport.summary: The horizontal line across the middle is the cell membrane: outside above, inside below. Add substances from the panel below and see what gets through and what does not. The later screens add more tools - channels then pumps.

screens.name: Simple Diffusion
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Only the things that can get through on their own, with no channels.

screens.name: Facilitated Diffusion
screens.what: Fit transport proteins into the membrane. With a channel, even ions get through.

screens.name: Active Transport
screens.what: Fit a pump. It spends energy to move things against the concentration.

screens.name: Playground
screens.what: Use all the tools freely.

controls.name: Solute Concentrations (below) - O₂ · CO₂ · Na⁺ · K⁺ · Glucose
controls.desc: Set how many of each substance to put outside and inside the cell.
controls.tip: Start with one substance only. Put several in at once and you cannot tell which is which.

controls.name: The membrane (the horizontal line in the middle)
controls.desc: A thin layer of fatty material with seven empty slots along the top for proteins.
controls.tip: On the Simple Diffusion screen the slots are empty. Oxygen and carbon dioxide still go straight through.

controls.name: The protein toolbox (top left)
controls.desc: Holds the transport proteins and pumps that go into the membrane. Drag one into a slot.
controls.tip: Each substance has its own channel. A sodium channel is what lets sodium through - any channel will not do.

controls.name: Crossing Highlights (checkbox, bottom right)
controls.desc: Flashes at the moment a substance crosses the membrane.
controls.tip: Leave it on. With many grains about it is hard to follow what crossed.

controls.name: Crossing Sounds (checkbox, bottom right)
controls.desc: Makes a sound as things cross.
controls.tip: You can tell whether the flow is lively without watching. As it approaches equilibrium the sounds thin out.

controls.name: Erase All Solutes (below)
controls.desc: Clears everything you have put in.
controls.tip: Clear it before moving on to the next substance, or it mixes with the last one and confuses you.

controls.name: The slow-speed and pause controls (below)
controls.desc: Play slowly or stop.
controls.tip: To watch the moment something passes through a channel, run it slowly.

steps: On the Simple Diffusion screen put O₂ outside the cell only.
Watch whether it goes straight through, until it is about even on both sides.
Clear it with Erase All Solutes and put Na⁺ outside only.
Confirm that it does not get through.
Try Glucose the same way.
On the Facilitated Diffusion screen fit a sodium channel and add it again.
Check which way it flows with a channel present.
On the Active Transport screen, fit a pump.
gotchas: Each substance has its own channel. Fit the wrong one and nothing gets through.
A channel only opens a door; it cannot change the direction. Things still flow from more to less.
Only a pump can push against the concentration, and it spends energy to do it.
A warning like Outside Sodium Too Low! at the top means you need to add more of the substance.
Clear things with Erase All Solutes before changing substance.

greenhouse-effect.summary: Compare the energy the Earth takes from the Sun against the energy it sends to space, as bars. The Energy Balance panel is the heart of this sim, so switch it on at the bottom right of the view before anything else.

screens.name: Waves
screens.what: Where this lesson starts. Draws the sunlight and the infrared as waves.

screens.name: Photons
screens.what: The same thing grain by grain. Where things turn back is clearer.

screens.name: Layer Model
screens.what: Divides the atmosphere into layers and calculates. Much harder.

controls.name: Energy Balance (checkbox, bottom right of the view)
controls.desc: Switch it on and In · Out · Net bars appear at the top left of the view, measured at the top of the atmosphere.
controls.tip: The most important readout in this sim. Once the temperature settles, Net goes to 0 - the answer to this lesson is right there.

controls.name: Greenhouse Gas Concentration (right) - None ↔ Lots
controls.desc: Sets the amount of greenhouse gas in the atmosphere.
controls.tip: Wait for it to settle at None and note the temperature, then push it to Lots. Comparing the two settled temperatures is the lesson.

controls.name: The surface thermometer (bottom left)
controls.desc: Shows the surface temperature. You can choose K · °C · °F.
controls.tip: °C gives you the feel. With no greenhouse gas it is about −28 °C, and the real Earth being 15 °C is thanks to the greenhouse effect.

controls.name: Start Sunlight (middle)
controls.desc: Switches the sunlight on. Nothing happens at all until you press it.
controls.tip: The experiment begins here. Do not be puzzled that the temperature will not move before you press it.

controls.name: Energy (right) - Sunlight · Infrared
controls.desc: Turns the two kinds of light on and off separately.
controls.tip: Try Infrared alone. It shows plainly that infrared is all the greenhouse gas catches. Sunlight goes straight through.

controls.name: The concentration mode chooser (under the concentration box, two picture buttons)
controls.desc: Chooses whether to set the greenhouse gas by amount or by period. There are no words - the left is by amount and the right, the calendar picture, is by period.
controls.tip: Switch to the calendar and you can choose Ice Age · 1750 · 1950 · 2020. Worth noting the temperature for each period and comparing.

controls.name: Cloud (checkbox, bottom right)
controls.desc: Puts a cloud in the sky.
controls.tip: A cloud works the opposite way to a greenhouse gas. It turns sunlight back and reduces In. Switch it on and off and compare the temperature.

controls.name: The flux meter (Photons screen)
controls.desc: Set a height and it measures the energy passing that level.
controls.tip: Move it up and down to see at what height the infrared drops off, which tells you where the greenhouse gas is acting.

controls.name: The slow-speed and step controls (below)
controls.desc: Play slowly or advance a frame at a time.
controls.tip: To catch one grain turning back on the Photons screen, run it slowly.

steps: Tick Energy Balance at the bottom right of the view.
Press Start Sunlight to switch the sunlight on.
At None, wait for Net to reach 0 and note the temperature.
Push the concentration to Lots and watch the Out bar fall.
Leave it a good while until the temperature settles.
Note the Net and the temperature then, and compare with the first.
Switch the Cloud on and off and compare the temperature.
Switch to the calendar button under the concentration box and note the temperature for each period.
gotchas: Nothing happens at all until you press Start Sunlight.
The temperature takes time to settle. Do not keep fiddling because it does not move at once.
Net reaching 0 means what comes in and what goes out have become equal. It does not mean the energy is 0.
Greenhouse gases catch the infrared, not the sunlight. A cloud does the opposite and turns sunlight back.
The concentration mode chooser has no words on it - tell the two pictures apart. The temperature units are K · °C · °F.
The Layer Model screen is beyond this lesson.
